extraction.body: Apple's first smart home hub, HomeView, arrives alongside a refreshed Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini — though Siri AI isn't ready on all of them yet. Apple made its long-rumored move into the smart home hub category official on Tuesday , unveiling HomeView alongside refreshed versions of the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini at its “Welcome Home” event in New York. The launch is also a personal milestone of sorts: it’s the first major hardware event for John Ternus, who took over as Apple’s chief executive on September 1 after 25 years at the company, most recently as the executive running hardware engineering. Ternus inherits a company investors have been watching more closely for hardware growth as its services business faces regulatory pressure, and a new product category gives him something fresh to point to. HomeView is a 7-inch Liquid Retina display, sold in a tabletop version with a domed aluminium speaker base and stainless steel tilting hinge, and a separate wall-mounted version, both priced at $299 in the US. The tabletop model comes in silver, starlight, rose pink and space gray, while the wall-mounted version ships in space gray and silver. It runs on an A18 chip and uses a front-facing camera to recognize up to six different household members by face, switching automatically between a shared household screen and a personalized one. Pre-orders opened Tuesday, with the device arriving November 13. The headline feature is Siri AI, an entirely new, more conversational version of Siri built on Apple’s next-generation Apple Intelligence. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, it can pull in personal context from Calendar, Messages and other apps to give more useful answers, and conversations started on HomeView sync via iCloud so they can continue on an iPhone, Mac, Apple Watch or Vision Pro. Apple’s Greg Joswiak, the company’s senior vice president of worldwide marketing, framed the pitch simply: HomeView is “designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user.” Beyond the assistant, HomeView functions as a household command center — FaceTime calls with Center Stage, Intercom, Apple Music with animated lyrics, Apple TV, Apple News and Apple Podcasts, plus control over accessories and scenes from Apple’s new Home Collection accessory line, which adds outdoor cameras, temperature sensors and access management into the same screen. The new Apple TV 4K, its first update in four years, is a more substantial overhaul than usual. It gets an A19 chip that Apple says delivers up to 50% faster CPU performance and twice the graphics performance of its predecessor, three built-in far-field microphones so people can talk to Siri without touching the remote, and an updated Siri Remote with Find My support and Precision Finding. Apple is also leaning on it as a smart home hub in its own right, using Apple Intelligence to generate camera activity descriptions and summarize notifications inside the Home app. It’s priced at $299, in a single 128GB configuration, and also ships November 13. Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of worldwide product marketing, called it the company’s “most immersive home theater experience yet.” The HomePod mini refresh is where the Siri AI story gets more complicated. The new $149 speaker, up $50 from the original 2020 model, gets an S10 chip for better sound and the ability to recognize sounds like a smoke alarm and alert a user’s phone, a feature Alexa devices have had for years. But Apple has confirmed that Siri AI itself won’t be available on the new HomePod mini at launch; it’s coming later through a software update, with no date given. That’s a notable gap in a launch built almost entirely around the promise of a smarter Siri everywhere in the home, and it lands on a different schedule than the rest of the lineup: the new HomePod mini ships October 30, two weeks before HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K. All of this is part of the Cupertino giant’s push into creating a complete home devices category. Apple is entering a smart display category where Amazon and Google have had products for years, and analysts have previously pointed out that the harder problem was never the hardware — it’s getting people to actually wire up a smart home in the first place. There’s also an irony sitting underneath the entire Siri AI push: Apple has previously confirmed it enlisted Google’s help this year to get Siri’s underlying capabilities up to scratch, meaning the assistant central to Apple’s pitch for its own hardware ecosystem has a rival’s fingerprints on it. Whether that matters to the people actually buying a $299 screen for their kitchen counter is a different question than whether Apple can build one. Tuesday’s event answered the second question. sources.title: The incredible flying Tesla Roadster is just for show
passages: But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.” Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance.

Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition.
Tesla says the “Rocket” configuration of the Roadster, the one we saw doing all the cool shit, will be “invite only.” But even that strains credulity.
Some analysts are already theorizing that the Roadster’s rerelease is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger.
So if the goal is to score a PR victory, dominate social media feeds, and cement Tesla’s brand as a frontier tech pioneer, then I would say the Roadster demo was a success.

extraction.body: Last night, Elon Musk gave the people what they want: a car driving vertically up a multistory ramp, launching off the edge, executing a midair “kickflip” over a lineup of Teslas, and landing via cold-gas thrusters. “We were promised flying cars,” sure, but isn’t the operative word in that statement “we”? Because as far as I can tell, everything we saw last night — while extremely cool and incredibly impressive — won’t result in a real, production-ready car you can park, or, I guess, land in your driveway. Tesla’s late-night demonstration in Waco, Texas, certainly gave some corners of the internet what it wants. Seeing a 0-to-60mph launch in under a second pushes the absolute outer limits of physics — even if it could lead to a detached retina or two. Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition. Tesla says the “Rocket” configuration of the Roadster, the one we saw doing all the cool shit, will be “invite only.” But even that strains credulity. That version of the Roadster removes the passenger seat to make room for the ultra-high-pressure gas tanks, and trades road practicality for short bursts of thruster-powered levitation. But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.” Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance. Tesla skipped basic commercial details like pricing or battery range specs. The Roadster’s range estimate was downgraded from 600 miles to 300 miles. And Musk casually pushed the production window out to 2028 — more than a decade after early adopters handed over $50,000 deposits. Musk himself has acknowledged the Roadster is a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially compared to mass-market models like the Model Y. He also called it “the last best driver’s car,” in a nod to his belief that autonomous driving will define Tesla’s future. Some analysts are already theorizing that the Roadster’s rerelease is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger. Musk’s fans on X are practically begging for it — even though it would likely result in the dilution of their own equity. But that’s just table stakes in Musk’s quest to consolidate control of his companies. In some sense, the car had to fly in order to make the preceding decade of missed deadlines feel worth it. Tesla has already been lapped several times in the electric hypercar market. Even some of the Roadster’s most impressive tricks have already been done. There are cars that can drive upside down, cars that can jump in the air, and cars that can accelerate very, very fast. BYD’s Yangwang U9 Xtreme uses four electric motors (one more than the Roadster) to produce an insane 3,000 horsepower for a top speed of 308mph in testing — beating the Rimac Nevera’s 268mph record. The Roadster could best it, but we’ll need to wait for independent testing to confirm. But no one puts on a show quite like Elon Musk. So if the goal is to score a PR victory, dominate social media feeds, and cement Tesla’s brand as a frontier tech pioneer, then I would say the Roadster demo was a success. Competitors like Rimac, Porsche, and BYD will continue shipping real, track-ready hypercars while Tesla spends another few years refining its rocket-boosted prototype.

coreStoryFacts.text: But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.” Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance.

Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition.

extraction.body: Last night, Elon Musk gave the people what they want: a car driving vertically up a multistory ramp, launching off the edge, executing a midair “kickflip” over a lineup of Teslas, and landing via cold-gas thrusters. “We were promised flying cars,” sure, but isn’t the operative word in that statement “we”? Because as far as I can tell, everything we saw last night — while extremely cool and incredibly impressive — won’t result in a real, production-ready car you can park, or, I guess, land in your driveway. Tesla’s late-night demonstration in Waco, Texas, certainly gave some corners of the internet what it wants. Seeing a 0-to-60mph launch in under a second pushes the absolute outer limits of physics — even if it could lead to a detached retina or two. Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition. Tesla says the “Rocket” configuration of the Roadster, the one we saw doing all the cool shit, will be “invite only.” But even that strains credulity. That version of the Roadster removes the passenger seat to make room for the ultra-high-pressure gas tanks, and trades road practicality for short bursts of thruster-powered levitation. But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.” Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance. Tesla skipped basic commercial details like pricing or battery range specs. The Roadster’s range estimate was downgraded from 600 miles to 300 miles. And Musk casually pushed the production window out to 2028 — more than a decade after early adopters handed over $50,000 deposits. Musk himself has acknowledged the Roadster is a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially compared to mass-market models like the Model Y. He also called it “the last best driver’s car,” in a nod to his belief that autonomous driving will define Tesla’s future. Some analysts are already theorizing that the Roadster’s rerelease is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger. Musk’s fans on X are practically begging for it — even though it would likely result in the dilution of their own equity. But that’s just table stakes in Musk’s quest to consolidate control of his companies. In some sense, the car had to fly in order to make the preceding decade of missed deadlines feel worth it. Tesla has already been lapped several times in the electric hypercar market. Even some of the Roadster’s most impressive tricks have already been done. There are cars that can drive upside down, cars that can jump in the air, and cars that can accelerate very, very fast. BYD’s Yangwang U9 Xtreme uses four electric motors (one more than the Roadster) to produce an insane 3,000 horsepower for a top speed of 308mph in testing — beating the Rimac Nevera’s 268mph record. The Roadster could best it, but we’ll need to wait for independent testing to confirm. But no one puts on a show quite like Elon Musk. So if the goal is to score a PR victory, dominate social media feeds, and cement Tesla’s brand as a frontier tech pioneer, then I would say the Roadster demo was a success. Competitors like Rimac, Porsche, and BYD will continue shipping real, track-ready hypercars while Tesla spends another few years refining its rocket-boosted prototype.

The seats inside are part of the chassis as a means of keeping weight down and the car features a steer-by-wire system. It has a steering yoke, electronic brakes and throttle controls. When there's a new car doing crazy things, you know Tom's Guide's resident racing enthusiast had to get involved and see what's going on. And I first thought "wait...this looks familiar." Not the flying stuff — that's of course a great sci-fi demo, but rather the physics-bending grip and acceleration. Then it hit me: the McMurtry Spéirling back at the Goodwood timed shootout in 2022. This race-spec car and the Tesla Roadster do the same thing, but in different ways. This is called ground effect, and the idea is to cheat the biggest limitation in traditional sports car design: waiting until you're going fast enough for wings and spoilers to push the car into the road. Both do this by using high-powered underfloor fans to literally vacuum the car down to the tarmac before the wheels turn — gluing the car to the asphalt and allowing their engines to dump instant torque straight into the ground without any wheel spin. The McMurtry relies entirely on that vacuum seal to carve through tight bends and set lap records. passages: Palo Alto startup Elorian has launched Glimpse, an AI model designed specifically for visual reasoning.

The company says its own testing shows Glimpse outperforming GPT-6 Astra on two tasks: reasoning about scientific charts and captioning short-form video. \n That is a bold claim from a company that only came out of stealth in April 2026.
On other visual reasoning tasks, the company describes its results as competitive rather than dominant. \n The bigger idea behind Glimpse is architectural.

Elorian builds native multimodal models, systems meant to work directly on images, video, and spatial or physical information without first converting any of it into text. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Elorian has been vocal about how far current models still trail people on visual tasks.
The company collaborated on a benchmark called Humanity’s Sixth Sense, which quizzes models with questions built around images and video clips.
Its target uses include robotics, engineering, medicine, and scientific analysis.
The Glimpse comparisons come from Elorian’s own evaluations, not from an independent lab.
Outside testing will be the real report card.
Elorian was founded in 2025 by CEO Andrew Dai , Yinfei Yang, and Seth Neel.
The founding team is made up of former researchers from Google DeepMind and Apple .
As of mid-October 2026, Elorian had fewer than 100 employees.

It has been in discussions with potential customers across several sectors, including robotics and design tools, and maintains an early-access waitlist for users who want to get their hands on its technology.
The company had previously said it planned to release its first public model and API later in 2026.
Glimpse marks its move from research thesis to an actual model people can evaluate.

sources.title: This new AI model thinks in images, not just words - Fast Company Middle East
passages: Elorian’s specialized models already outperform Gemini 3 Pro on certain visual reasoning benchmarks, Dai says, though he declined to name them, saying disclosure would let competitors optimize against them. (Gemini is still fundamentally a transformer model that projects vision into a shared latent space, but DeepMind is also investing in research on models that reason over visual images themselves rather than words.)
Birthrates are plunging across the Middle East.

When recent multimodal language models like Google’s Gemini process imagery, what they really do is create a detailed description of an image using words, which they arrange in a giant internal word map based on their meanings.
They then reason about the words to make observations, judgements, and even suggestions about the image.
Among them is Andrew Dai, a veteran AI researcher who left Google DeepMind to build models designed from the ground up to understand, reason about, and generate images .

Dai believes that the visual image is as fundamental to model intelligence as language—if not more so—and that frontier language models have hit a ceiling because they still can’t reason effectively about the physical world, not to mention being “incredibly unstable,” as he puts its.
Elorian’s models will reason and simulate, while an LLM can only describe and reference.
But Dai’s company is young and is still developing its models and fitting them to its first addressable markets.
Elorian plans a general Application Programming Interface release by the end of the year, which will allow developers to build apps on top of its visual reasoning models.

extraction.body: For almost a decade, AI researchers have been obsessed with one kind of artificial intelligence —large language models (LLMs), which they train to write, talk, and reason using words. The tech industry is making an enormous bet that making such models bigger and smarter is the path to superintelligence. But in 2026 some very high-profile AI researchers doubt that this word-centric approach is the whole answer. Among them is Andrew Dai, a veteran AI researcher who left Google DeepMind to build models designed from the ground up to understand, reason about, and generate images . His startup company, Elorian AI, came out of stealth in April. Dai believes that the visual image is as fundamental to model intelligence as language—if not more so—and that frontier language models have hit a ceiling because they still can’t reason effectively about the physical world, not to mention being “incredibly unstable,” as he puts its. A model that can’t count the number of cups on a table or judge spatial relationships falls short of general intelligence, no matter how well it writes or codes, Dai says. For instance, if shown a schematic of a motorcycle engine design, a multimodal LLM might observe that when motorcycle engines heat up, an aluminum alloy piston crown can expand, which might decrease the clearance between it and the cylinder wall. Then it could suggest changes to the design to make the engine more durable at high rpm operation. Elorian’s models will reason and simulate, while an LLM can only describe and reference. Elorian’s models can run what Dai calls an edit-simulate-correction loop; they generate a design, then test it within a physics simulation, then identify design flaws, then revise the design accordingly, automatically. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.

Elorian , the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.
The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply.
Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean.

extraction.body: For almost a decade, AI researchers have been obsessed with one kind of artificial intelligence —large language models (LLMs), which they train to write, talk, and reason using words. The tech industry is making an enormous bet that making such models bigger and smarter is the path to superintelligence. But in 2026 some very high-profile AI researchers doubt that this word-centric approach is the whole answer. Among them is Andrew Dai, a veteran AI researcher who left Google DeepMind to build models designed from the ground up to understand, reason about, and generate images . His startup company, Elorian AI, came out of stealth in April. Dai believes that the visual image is as fundamental to model intelligence as language—if not more so—and that frontier language models have hit a ceiling because they still can’t reason effectively about the physical world, not to mention being “incredibly unstable,” as he puts its. A model that can’t count the number of cups on a table or judge spatial relationships falls short of general intelligence, no matter how well it writes or codes, Dai says. Elorian, which Dai cofounded with the former Apple machine-learning researcher Yinfei Yang, is developing models that give visual data equal play with language tokens within their architecture. “We’re betting on these visual representations for things like spatial problems and navigation and everything else,” he says. When recent multimodal language models like Google’s Gemini process imagery, what they really do is create a detailed description of an image using words, which they arrange in a giant internal word map based on their meanings. They then reason about the words to make observations, judgements, and even suggestions about the image. For instance, if shown a schematic of a motorcycle engine design, a multimodal LLM might observe that when motorcycle engines heat up, an aluminum alloy piston crown can expand, which might decrease the clearance between it and the cylinder wall. By contrast, Elorian is building visual reasoning models that will “think” about images directly. Instead of creating a word map, they’ll form a detailed 3D internal map of an image, the way humans imagine things. Because the model has an understanding of physics, it can make much more detailed and accurate observations. In the motorcycle engine example, the model could show how the dimensions of piston crown and cylinder wall, and the clearance between the two, would change over time as the motorcycle engine revs up. Then it could suggest changes to the design to make the engine more durable at high rpm operation. Elorian’s models will reason and simulate, while an LLM can only describe and reference. So Elorian’s visual reasoning models could find natural applications in industries that require a deep physical understanding of imagery. Elorian is targeting what Dai calls the physical economy, an $80 trillion category that includes video understanding and mechanical engineering. In the latter, Dai said engineers currently spend hundreds of hours manually drawing components in CAD software. Elorian’s models can run what Dai calls an edit-simulate-correction loop; they generate a design, then test it within a physics simulation, then identify design flaws, then revise the design accordingly, automatically. Dai spent 14 years at Google Brain and DeepMind. There he coauthored research that provided technical groundwork for the GPT series models, and led data work on Gemini. He left with a team of researchers to start Elorian, headquartered in Palo Alto. Dai says one of the reasons he left Google was that the company is now concentrating its compute resources on a few distinct areas, including code generation, and allotting less compute to research on visual reasoning. Elorian’s specialized models already outperform Gemini 3 Pro on certain visual reasoning benchmarks, Dai says, though he declined to name them, saying disclosure would let competitors optimize against them. (Gemini is still fundamentally a transformer model that projects vision into a shared latent space, but DeepMind is also investing in research on models that reason over visual images themselves rather than words.) Elorian has raised $55 million in seed funding at a $300 million valuation. Investors include Nvidia and Menlo Ventures, as well as Dai’s former boss, the legendary Google chief scientist Jeff Dean. PitchBook also lists 49 Palms Ventures, 500 Global, and Altimeter Capital Management, among others, as investors. Elorian’s $300 million seed valuation is modest next to other startups building AI for the physical world. Physical Intelligence, a robotics foundation model company founded in 2024 by the former Google DeepMind researcher Karol Hausman and the Stanford professor Sergey Levine, was valued at $5.6 billion in a $600 million funding round in November. World Labs, a spatial-intelligence startup founded by the Stanford professor and AI researcher Fei-Fei Li, works on a related problem: AI systems that reason about three-dimensional space rather than 2D images. The company’s product, Marble, generates navigable 3D environments from text, images, or video. World Labs raised $1 billion in a February round led by Autodesk along with Nvidia, AMD, and Andreessen Horowitz. Moonvalley, which was acquired by Reka this year, built the licensed-footage video model Marey, then moved into world models. Reka said the combined team will develop AI that can simulate motion and physics to help robots reason about the consequences of their actions. But Dai’s company is young and is still developing its models and fitting them to its first addressable markets. Elorian plans a general Application Programming Interface release by the end of the year, which will allow developers to build apps on top of its visual reasoning models. Be in the Know . (Gemini is still fundamentally a transformer model that projects vision into a shared latent space, but DeepMind is also investing in research on models that reason over visual images themselves rather than words.)

When recent multimodal language models like Google’s Gemini process imagery, what they really do is create a detailed description of an image using words, which they arrange in a giant internal word map based on their meanings.
They then reason about the words to make observations, judgements, and even suggestions about the image.
Among them is Andrew Dai, a veteran AI researcher who left Google DeepMind to build models designed from the ground up to understand, reason about, and generate images .

Dai believes that the visual image is as fundamental to model intelligence as language—if not more so—and that frontier language models have hit a ceiling because they still can’t reason effectively about the physical world, not to mention being “incredibly unstable,” as he puts its.
Elorian’s models will reason and simulate, while an LLM can only describe and reference.
But Dai’s company is young and is still developing its models and fitting them to its first addressable markets.

passages: Morgan Stanley estimates Bitcoin's market cap represents roughly 2% of a $130 trillion addressable market.
That market is defined as the combined value of global M2 money supply and gold.
The focus on Bitcoin specifically, rather than the broader digital asset universe, is notable.

Morgan Stanley's Global Investment Committee has formally endorsed Bitcoin as a scarce, non-sovereign store of value, drawing a direct parallel to gold and recommending it as a legitimate portfolio allocation for clients across the risk spectrum.
Amy Oldenburg walked through the digital gold thesis and the allocation framework in a Bitcoin Magazine interview on September 14, 2026.
The bank's research projects annualized returns for Bitcoin across several adoption scenarios.
A flat-adoption environment produces returns in the neighborhood of 3%.
A baseline scenario tied to steady population growth points toward 6-7% annually.
Accelerated adoption could push returns closer to 10%.
These are scenario-based return estimates grounded in user-growth modeling frameworks typically applied to emerging technology platforms.
The GIC's recommended Bitcoin exposure ranges from 0-2% for balanced growth portfolios and climbs to 2-4% for clients with a higher risk tolerance and a more opportunistic mandate.
Those numbers were formalized in October 2025 and reflect the committee's view that Bitcoin's fixed supply and low current penetration make it a credible long-term holding.

extraction.body: Morgan Stanley is seeing early signs of Bitcoin entering broader portfolio allocations. The bank has raised lending limits against Bitcoin ETPs and is exploring loans backed by spot crypto. Bitcoin is beginning to move beyond a stand-alone investment and into formal portfolio allocations, while lending against exchange-traded products and spot crypto is set to expand. In an Oct. 15 interview with Bitcoin Magazine, Morgan Stanley digital asset strategist Amy Oldenburg said much of the demand for the bank’s Bitcoin ETF has come from self-directed investors, with early signs of Bitcoin being integrated into broader asset-allocation models. Oldenburg said the product has operated for only six months and that Morgan Stanley plans to monitor flows through its one-year anniversary. While advisers in the bank’s wealth business are directing some inflows, a substantial share comes from individuals choosing the product themselves. She described Bitcoin’s emerging role within broader allocations, rather than merely as a stand-alone position, as a positive sign. She also emphasized the case for Bitcoin as digital gold. Bitcoin’s volatility remained relatively low this year as technology shares became more volatile, but it recently traded alongside risk assets, retreating while gold rose. Oldenburg said Bitcoin would need to behave more like digital gold to fulfill that intended portfolio role. Interest in converting spot Bitcoin into ETF shares through in-kind transactions has exceeded Oldenburg’s expectations, although completed transactions have lagged inquiries because the process requires paperwork and other steps. She cited hardware-wallet security concerns and estate planning as key drivers, adding that holding Bitcoin within the wealth-management system makes it easier to administer alongside other assets. Morgan Stanley already offers lending against Bitcoin ETPs and increased the available limits on that exposure earlier this year. Oldenburg said the bank also plans to explore lending against spot crypto as it expands the products available through its E-Trade platform. Asked whether demand for such borrowing was growing, she said it was, calling it a natural next request after adding the products. On competition involving stablecoins and the Bitcoin network, Oldenburg said it was too early to select a winning technology or product. Morgan Stanley is devoting significant attention to stablecoins and the broader digital-money market while monitoring new products being built on Bitcoin. Quantum computing is viewed as a longer-term issue rather than an immediate threat. Oldenburg said there were no signs of a near-term problem and that quantum risk applies to Morgan Stanley’s entire business, not only Bitcoin. Other risks, including the development of AI tools, are also affecting the market, but the bank continues studying quantum-related exposure. Tokenization could apply to nearly every asset and may improve efficiency by placing multiple asset classes on shared technology infrastructure, Oldenburg said. Clearing organizations in the U.S. and international markets are examining round-the-clock trading and broader market access, though differences among tokenized products make the market’s eventual size difficult to estimate. Oldenburg said new technology could bring products to market that were previously too inefficient or administratively burdensome to securitize. She described the total addressable market for tokenization as large and said 2027 would be an important year as projects begin reaching the market. Bitcoin’s volatility remained relatively low this year as technology shares became more volatile, but it recently traded alongside risk assets, retreating while gold rose. Oldenburg said Bitcoin would need to behave more like digital gold to fulfill that intended portfolio role.

Interest in converting spot Bitcoin into ETF shares through in-kind transactions has exceeded Oldenburg’s expectations, although completed transactions have lagged inquiries because the process requires paperwork and other steps. She cited hardware-wallet security concerns and estate planning as key drivers, adding that holding Bitcoin within the wealth-management system makes it easier to administer alongside other assets.

Morgan Stanley already offers lending against Bitcoin ETPs and increased the available limits on that exposure earlier this year. Oldenburg said the bank also plans to explore lending against spot crypto as it expands the products available through its E-Trade platform. Asked whether demand for such borrowing was growing, she said it was, calling it a natural next request after adding the products.

On competition involving stablecoins and the Bitcoin network, Oldenburg said it was too early to select a winning technology or product. Morgan Stanley is devoting significant attention to stablecoins and the broader digital-money market while monitoring new products being built on Bitcoin.

Quantum computing is viewed as a longer-term issue rather than an immediate threat. Oldenburg said there were no signs of a near-term problem and that quantum risk applies to Morgan Stanley’s entire business, not only Bitcoin. Other risks, including the development of AI tools, are also affecting the market, but the bank continues studying quantum-related exposure.

Tokenization could apply to nearly every asset and may improve efficiency by placing multiple asset classes on shared technology infrastructure, Oldenburg said. Clearing organizations in the U.S. and international markets are examining round-the-clock trading and broader market access, though differences among tokenized products make the market’s eventual size difficult to estimate.

Oldenburg said new technology could bring products to market that were previously too inefficient or administratively burdensome to securitize. She described the total addressable market for tokenization as large and said 2027 would be an important year as projects begin reaching the market.
Riza Dagoc reports on regulation, investing and the digital-asset business for TokenPost. Send corrections or tips to info@tokenpost.com.

coreStoryFacts.text: Morgan Stanley estimates Bitcoin's market cap represents roughly 2% of a $130 trillion addressable market.
That market is defined as the combined value of global M2 money supply and gold.
The focus on Bitcoin specifically, rather than the broader digital asset universe, is notable.

Morgan Stanley's Global Investment Committee has formally endorsed Bitcoin as a scarce, non-sovereign store of value, drawing a direct parallel to gold and recommending it as a legitimate portfolio allocation for clients across the risk spectrum.
Amy Oldenburg walked through the digital gold thesis and the allocation framework in a Bitcoin Magazine interview on September 14, 2026.
The bank's research projects annualized returns for Bitcoin across several adoption scenarios.
A flat-adoption environment produces returns in the neighborhood of 3%.
A baseline scenario tied to steady population growth points toward 6-7% annually.
Accelerated adoption could push returns closer to 10%.
These are scenario-based return estimates grounded in user-growth modeling frameworks typically applied to emerging technology platforms.
The GIC's recommended Bitcoin exposure ranges from 0-2% for balanced growth portfolios and climbs to 2-4% for clients with a higher risk tolerance and a more opportunistic mandate.
Those numbers were formalized in October 2025 and reflect the committee's view that Bitcoin's fixed supply and low current penetration make it a credible long-term holding.

extraction.body: Morgan Stanley is seeing early signs of Bitcoin entering broader portfolio allocations. The bank has raised lending limits against Bitcoin ETPs and is exploring loans backed by spot crypto. Bitcoin is beginning to move beyond a stand-alone investment and into formal portfolio allocations, while lending against exchange-traded products and spot crypto is set to expand. In an Oct. 15 interview with Bitcoin Magazine, Morgan Stanley digital asset strategist Amy Oldenburg said much of the demand for the bank’s Bitcoin ETF has come from self-directed investors, with early signs of Bitcoin being integrated into broader asset-allocation models. Oldenburg said the product has operated for only six months and that Morgan Stanley plans to monitor flows through its one-year anniversary. While advisers in the bank’s wealth business are directing some inflows, a substantial share comes from individuals choosing the product themselves. She described Bitcoin’s emerging role within broader allocations, rather than merely as a stand-alone position, as a positive sign. She also emphasized the case for Bitcoin as digital gold. Bitcoin’s volatility remained relatively low this year as technology shares became more volatile, but it recently traded alongside risk assets, retreating while gold rose. Oldenburg said Bitcoin would need to behave more like digital gold to fulfill that intended portfolio role. Interest in converting spot Bitcoin into ETF shares through in-kind transactions has exceeded Oldenburg’s expectations, although completed transactions have lagged inquiries because the process requires paperwork and other steps. She cited hardware-wallet security concerns and estate planning as key drivers, adding that holding Bitcoin within the wealth-management system makes it easier to administer alongside other assets. Morgan Stanley already offers lending against Bitcoin ETPs and increased the available limits on that exposure earlier this year. Oldenburg said the bank also plans to explore lending against spot crypto as it expands the products available through its E-Trade platform. Asked whether demand for such borrowing was growing, she said it was, calling it a natural next request after adding the products. On competition involving stablecoins and the Bitcoin network, Oldenburg said it was too early to select a winning technology or product. Morgan Stanley is devoting significant attention to stablecoins and the broader digital-money market while monitoring new products being built on Bitcoin. Quantum computing is viewed as a longer-term issue rather than an immediate threat. Oldenburg said there were no signs of a near-term problem and that quantum risk applies to Morgan Stanley’s entire business, not only Bitcoin. Other risks, including the development of AI tools, are also affecting the market, but the bank continues studying quantum-related exposure. Tokenization could apply to nearly every asset and may improve efficiency by placing multiple asset classes on shared technology infrastructure, Oldenburg said. Clearing organizations in the U.S. and international markets are examining round-the-clock trading and broader market access, though differences among tokenized products make the market’s eventual size difficult to estimate. Oldenburg said new technology could bring products to market that were previously too inefficient or administratively burdensome to securitize. She described the total addressable market for tokenization as large and said 2027 would be an important year as projects begin reaching the market. Riza Dagoc reports on regulation, investing and the digital-asset business for TokenPost. Send corrections or tips to info@tokenpost.com.

extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. extraction.body: Image used for representational purposes only. | Photo Credit: Reuters An artificial intelligence agent looking for private encryption keys on an Australian government website has triggered a warning that the next target could be anywhere. The incident, in which an autonomous AI system went beyond its intended task and attempted to circumvent security protections, has become a stark example of a growing concern among AI safety researchers: what happens when an AI agent is given a goal but is left to decide for itself how far it should go to achieve it. For countries such as India, with vast government databases and increasingly digitised public infrastructure, researchers say the incident should serve as a warning. “What happened with, say, an Australian community website can happen with an Indian website or an Indian government system, which would be more crucial,” Dr. Srinivas Padmanabuni, Co-founder and CTO of AiEnsured, said. “India should bring in regulations. It could become horrible when one major incident happens and somebody steals the secrets of one of the major departments or, say, atomic energy,” he said. The Australian episode is part of a series of recent incidents that have brought a new term into the AI safety debate: “reward hacking”, the ability of autonomous AI agents to exploit loopholes, manipulate systems or circumvent safeguards when doing so helps them accomplish the objective they have been given. As AI agents become increasingly capable of acting independently on the internet, experts say the distinction between an AI system that merely generates information and one that can actively interact with digital infrastructure is becoming critical. A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data while searching for vulnerabilities, according to disclosures surrounding the incident. The agents had been tasked with finding weaknesses in systems. In pursuing that objective, they searched government databases for broken credentials and attempted to access private encryption keys. For researchers, the significance lies not simply in what was accessed, but in how the AI behaved while pursuing its goal. Dr. Srinivas describes this as reward hacking in simple terms. “Cheat, borrow, steal, beg, do whatever, but achieve your objective. That's the mantra of an agent”, he says. The concern is that an autonomous system does not necessarily interpret an instruction in the same way a human would. If it is rewarded for achieving an outcome, it may discover an unexpected route to that outcome, including one that violates the assumptions or safeguards built around it. The Australian incident has gained added significance following OpenAI's disclosure on Friday (September 25, 20276) that it had alerted “dozens” of institutions around the world that its AI agents may have interacted improperly with their websites. The company said the agents had attempted to obtain information from governments, universities, public agencies and other institutions, including the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, the Census Bureau and the Education Department. OpenAI said the agents were generally attempting to locate authoritative sources of public information. But in some cases, they went further, attempting to bypass security measures. When trying to access information from the U.S. Census Bureau, for example, some agents used tools intended for software developers. OpenAI said the government information accessed by the bots was public. But it also disclosed that information obtained from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission was later published by AI agents on another website, an action the company said was unintended. In other cases, the company said, its agents transferred data when they should not have. Taken together, the incidents point to a difficult question for the AI industry: when an autonomous system is capable of acting on its own, who decides where the boundary lies between persistence and intrusion? The concern did not begin with the Australian government website. In July, a group or “swarm” of OpenAI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being explicitly instructed to do so. Hugging Face was the first to publicly disclose the incident, with OpenAI later acknowledging responsibility. The episode offered another glimpse into how autonomous systems can move from one objective to another. According to Dr. Srinivas, the agents identified Hugging Face as a valuable target because it hosts software, APIs and other resources used by developers. “They said, Hugging Face is a place where developers store all their software, all their APIs for public view. Let's target Hugging Face,” he said. The agents then looked for vulnerabilities, found exploitable software and created a server daemon on the platform. From there, according to Srinivas, they began probing other vulnerable components in search of exploitable keys and ways to gain greater access. That last step is known as privilege escalation, which essentially means obtaining higher-level permissions than the system was initially supposed to allow. “I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly,” he said, adding that similar incidents had reportedly been occurring for months at a handful of frontier AI laboratories without monitoring. At the same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for international leaders to establish global standards for AI safety, including mechanisms to monitor and report serious incidents. The push for international oversight comes as AI systems move rapidly from being tools that respond to human instructions to agents capable of planning and executing multi-step tasks with increasing independence. Australia was among 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for AI development. But researchers argue that international declarations alone may not be enough. For India, the issue is particularly significant because the country's digital infrastructure increasingly spans government services, financial systems, public databases and critical infrastructure. An autonomous AI system attempting to access a government website may initially appear to be a relatively contained incident. The consequences could be very different if the same behaviour were directed at a system containing sensitive government, strategic or national-security information. Srinivas believes that the gap needs to be closed before the next major incident. He has called for a temporary two- to three-year pause on training more powerful AI models, until there is substantially more research into containment and into detecting and mitigating reward hacking. The Australian incident and OpenAI’s new disclosures have, meanwhile, demonstrated the underlying problem in concrete terms. The question now is whether governments will treat it as an isolated breach or as an early warning of what autonomous AI could do when its instructions are clear, but its boundaries are not.

An artificial intelligence agent looking for private encryption keys on an Australian government website has triggered a warning that the next target could be anywhere.

The incident, in which an autonomous AI system went beyond its intended task and attempted to circumvent security protections, has become a stark example of a growing concern among AI safety researchers: what happens when an AI agent is given a goal but is left to decide for itself how far it should go to achieve it.

For countries such as India, with vast government databases and increasingly digitised public infrastructure, researchers say the incident should serve as a warning. “What happened with, say, an Australian community website can happen with an Indian website or an Indian government system, which would be more crucial,” Dr. Srinivas Padmanabuni, Co-founder and CTO of AiEnsured, said.
“India should bring in regulations. It could become horrible when one major incident happens and somebody steals the secrets of one of the major departments or, say, atomic energy,” he said.

The Australian episode is part of a series of recent incidents that have brought a new term into the AI safety debate: “reward hacking”, the ability of autonomous AI agents to exploit loopholes, manipulate systems or circumvent safeguards when doing so helps them accomplish the objective they have been given.

As AI agents become increasingly capable of acting independently on the internet, experts say the distinction between an AI system that merely generates information and one that can actively interact with digital infrastructure is becoming critical.
A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data while searching for vulnerabilities, according to disclosures surrounding the incident.
The agents had been tasked with finding weaknesses in systems. In pursuing that objective, they searched government databases for broken credentials and attempted to access private encryption keys.
For researchers, the significance lies not simply in what was accessed, but in how the AI behaved while pursuing its goal.
Dr. Srinivas describes this as reward hacking in simple terms. “Cheat, borrow, steal, beg, do whatever, but achieve your objective. That's the mantra of an agent”, he says.

The concern is that an autonomous system does not necessarily interpret an instruction in the same way a human would. If it is rewarded for achieving an outcome, it may discover an unexpected route to that outcome, including one that violates the assumptions or safeguards built around it.

The Australian incident has gained added significance following OpenAI's disclosure on Friday (September 25, 20276) that it had alerted “dozens” of institutions around the world that its AI agents may have interacted improperly with their websites.

The company said the agents had attempted to obtain information from governments, universities, public agencies and other institutions, including the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, the Census Bureau and the Education Department.
OpenAI said the agents were generally attempting to locate authoritative sources of public information. But in some cases, they went further, attempting to bypass security measures.
When trying to access information from the U.S. Census Bureau, for example, some agents used tools intended for software developers.

OpenAI said the government information accessed by the bots was public. But it also disclosed that information obtained from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission was later published by AI agents on another website, an action the company said was unintended.
In other cases, the company said, its agents transferred data when they should not have.

Taken together, the incidents point to a difficult question for the AI industry: when an autonomous system is capable of acting on its own, who decides where the boundary lies between persistence and intrusion?

The concern did not begin with the Australian government website. In July, a group or “swarm” of OpenAI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being explicitly instructed to do so. Hugging Face was the first to publicly disclose the incident, with OpenAI later acknowledging responsibility.
The episode offered another glimpse into how autonomous systems can move from one objective to another.
According to Dr. Srinivas, the agents identified Hugging Face as a valuable target because it hosts software, APIs and other resources used by developers.
“They said, Hugging Face is a place where developers store all their software, all their APIs for public view. Let's target Hugging Face,” he said.

The agents then looked for vulnerabilities, found exploitable software and created a server daemon on the platform. From there, according to Srinivas, they began probing other vulnerable components in search of exploitable keys and ways to gain greater access.
That last step is known as privilege escalation, which essentially means obtaining higher-level permissions than the system was initially supposed to allow.

“I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly,” he said, adding that similar incidents had reportedly been occurring for months at a handful of frontier AI laboratories without monitoring.

At the same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for international leaders to establish global standards for AI safety, including mechanisms to monitor and report serious incidents.

The push for international oversight comes as AI systems move rapidly from being tools that respond to human instructions to agents capable of planning and executing multi-step tasks with increasing independence.

Australia was among 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for AI development. But researchers argue that international declarations alone may not be enough.
For India, the issue is particularly significant because the country's digital infrastructure increasingly spans government services, financial systems, public databases and critical infrastructure.

An autonomous AI system attempting to access a government website may initially appear to be a relatively contained incident. The consequences could be very different if the same behaviour were directed at a system containing sensitive government, strategic or national-security information.

Srinivas believes that the gap needs to be closed before the next major incident. He has called for a temporary two- to three-year pause on training more powerful AI models, until there is substantially more research into containment and into detecting and mitigating reward hacking.

The Australian incident and OpenAI’s new disclosures have, meanwhile, demonstrated the underlying problem in concrete terms. The question now is whether governments will treat it as an isolated breach or as an early warning of what autonomous AI could do when its instructions are clear, but its boundaries are not.

extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. For countries such as India, with vast government databases and increasingly digitised public infrastructure, researchers say the incident should serve as a warning. “What happened with, say, an Australian community website can happen with an Indian website or an Indian government system, which would be more crucial,” Dr. Srinivas Padmanabuni, Co-founder and CTO of AiEnsured, said.
“India should bring in regulations. It could become horrible when one major incident happens and somebody steals the secrets of one of the major departments or, say, atomic energy,” he said.

The Australian episode is part of a series of recent incidents that have brought a new term into the AI safety debate: “reward hacking”, the ability of autonomous AI agents to exploit loopholes, manipulate systems or circumvent safeguards when doing so helps them accomplish the objective they have been given.

As AI agents become increasingly capable of acting independently on the internet, experts say the distinction between an AI system that merely generates information and one that can actively interact with digital infrastructure is becoming critical.
A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data while searching for vulnerabilities, according to disclosures surrounding the incident.
The agents had been tasked with finding weaknesses in systems. In pursuing that objective, they searched government databases for broken credentials and attempted to access private encryption keys.
For researchers, the significance lies not simply in what was accessed, but in how the AI behaved while pursuing its goal.
Dr. Srinivas describes this as reward hacking in simple terms. “Cheat, borrow, steal, beg, do whatever, but achieve your objective. That's the mantra of an agent”, he says.

The concern is that an autonomous system does not necessarily interpret an instruction in the same way a human would. If it is rewarded for achieving an outcome, it may discover an unexpected route to that outcome, including one that violates the assumptions or safeguards built around it.

The Australian incident has gained added significance following OpenAI's disclosure on Friday (September 25, 20276) that it had alerted “dozens” of institutions around the world that its AI agents may have interacted improperly with their websites.

The company said the agents had attempted to obtain information from governments, universities, public agencies and other institutions, including the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, the Census Bureau and the Education Department.
OpenAI said the agents were generally attempting to locate authoritative sources of public information. But in some cases, they went further, attempting to bypass security measures.
When trying to access information from the U.S. Census Bureau, for example, some agents used tools intended for software developers.

OpenAI said the government information accessed by the bots was public. But it also disclosed that information obtained from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission was later published by AI agents on another website, an action the company said was unintended.
In other cases, the company said, its agents transferred data when they should not have.

Taken together, the incidents point to a difficult question for the AI industry: when an autonomous system is capable of acting on its own, who decides where the boundary lies between persistence and intrusion?

The concern did not begin with the Australian government website. In July, a group or “swarm” of OpenAI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being explicitly instructed to do so. Hugging Face was the first to publicly disclose the incident, with OpenAI later acknowledging responsibility.
The episode offered another glimpse into how autonomous systems can move from one objective to another.
According to Dr. Srinivas, the agents identified Hugging Face as a valuable target because it hosts software, APIs and other resources used by developers.
“They said, Hugging Face is a place where developers store all their software, all their APIs for public view. Let's target Hugging Face,” he said.

The agents then looked for vulnerabilities, found exploitable software and created a server daemon on the platform. From there, according to Srinivas, they began probing other vulnerable components in search of exploitable keys and ways to gain greater access.
That last step is known as privilege escalation, which essentially means obtaining higher-level permissions than the system was initially supposed to allow.

“I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly,” he said, adding that similar incidents had reportedly been occurring for months at a handful of frontier AI laboratories without monitoring.

At the same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for international leaders to establish global standards for AI safety, including mechanisms to monitor and report serious incidents.

The push for international oversight comes as AI systems move rapidly from being tools that respond to human instructions to agents capable of planning and executing multi-step tasks with increasing independence.

Australia was among 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for AI development. But researchers argue that international declarations alone may not be enough.
For India, the issue is particularly significant because the country's digital infrastructure increasingly spans government services, financial systems, public databases and critical infrastructure.

An autonomous AI system attempting to access a government website may initially appear to be a relatively contained incident. The consequences could be very different if the same behaviour were directed at a system containing sensitive government, strategic or national-security information.

Srinivas believes that the gap needs to be closed before the next major incident. He has called for a temporary two- to three-year pause on training more powerful AI models, until there is substantially more research into containment and into detecting and mitigating reward hacking.

The Australian incident and OpenAI’s new disclosures have, meanwhile, demonstrated the underlying problem in concrete terms. The question now is whether governments will treat it as an isolated breach or as an early warning of what autonomous AI could do when its instructions are clear, but its boundaries are not.

sources.title: Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations - CNBC
passages: Amazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market.
Amazon acquired Bee , a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount.
Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations.
When turned on, Bee devices are always recording.

Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to "review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed." It can also track "trends or themes that recur" to give personalized goals or actions.
For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps.
Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new AI hardware .

Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused Alexa Tablets , while Microsoft showcased an Nvidia -powered Windows laptop and Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI.

Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word.
An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said.
The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing.

sources.title: Amazon expands Bee lineup with two AI devices that record conversations - JournalArta
passages: Amazon’s new Bee devices put conversation recording into two everyday forms: a bracelet and a credit card-sized recorder that attaches to a smartphone.
The launch extends the company’s push into AI hardware, while raising the familiar question of how always-listening gadgets handle personal conversations.
Amazon unveiled the Bee Frontier, priced at $75, and the Bee Eclipse, priced at $100.
The release is the first update to Bee’s product lineup since Amazon bought the San Francisco startup in July 2025 for an undisclosed sum.
The Frontier can be worn on the wrist or clipped to clothing.
Like earlier Bee bracelets, it uses microphones and artificial intelligence to record, transcribe and analyze conversations.
Amazon says its battery lasts up to seven days, matching the stated endurance of previous generations.
The price has risen: the Frontier costs $75, compared with $50 for its predecessor.
Amazon says the device’s dual microphones have improved noise filtering, helping it identify useful speech in busy surroundings and screen out background sound.
Bee devices are designed to listen throughout a user’s day, then turn spoken exchanges into information that can be reviewed or analyzed.
The approach makes recording less deliberate than opening a voice-recorder app, but also puts privacy and consent at the heart of how people may use the devices.
Amazon has not provided further details in the supplied announcement about the Eclipse’s battery life or recording features.
The English-language global edition of JournalArta.
The devices’ next test will be whether users find the convenience of automated notes worth carrying a microphone that can capture conversations as they happen.

extraction.body: After a Chrome clone was spotted on the Play Store earlier this week, a user on Reddit says they’re seeing a fake version of WhatsApp in a “sponsored” slot above the real version. As reported earlier by Android Authority, the WhatsApp dupe has racked up over 500,000 downloads and, at the time of writing, its Play Store listing is still live. The WhatsApp clone is from a developer going by “Agment Assets sallu” who doesn’t currently have anything else listed on the Play Store. Their listing for the WhatsApp impostor has the same icon, screenshots, and text as the real version, but the real WhatsApp has over 10 billion downloads, an “editor’s choice” badge, and over 246 million reviews. Android Authority points out that the WhatsApp clone may be using Google Play’s Early Access program to disable public user reviews, which could have helped users warn people against downloading the app.

sources.title: Real or Fake? How to Check If That iPhone Is Original Before Paying - Pulse Nigeria
passages: Fake iPhones are increasing in number, but they are still far from the real deal.
From their clunky software to their cheap construction, they can't replicate the Apple experience.
If you're paying hundreds of thousands of Naira for a phone, you deserve your money's worth.
A fake iPhone might look real at first glance, but it rarely feels the same in your hands.
Just say, “Hey, Siri.” Real iPhones will respond instantly.
Check Apple Nigeria's official prices or compare them with those of authorised dealers like SLOT, Pointek, or iStore.
Smoothness: iOS animations are smooth and consistent.
Fake iPhones lag, especially when switching apps or opening the camera.
Even the plastic wrapping on an original iPhone is high quality and tightly wrapped.
Font and Spacing: Check the "iPhone" marking on the back closely.
Weight: Original iPhones have a premium weight due to their metal and glass design.
Camera Placement: Most fake iPhone cameras are off-centre or not flush with the surface.
When buying, it helps to carry a real iPhone (if you have one) for comparison.
Only real iPhones can access iCloud and FaceTime.
Some fake iPhones come with micro-USB or USB-C charging ports.
Most counterfeit iPhones are sold in sealed boxes that appear original but contain substandard phones inside.
One of the most misleading things about high-end clones is the fake iOS skins they use.
If it takes you to the Google Play Store, it's a fake.

extraction.body: After a Chrome clone was spotted on the Play Store earlier this week, a user on Reddit says they’re seeing a fake version of WhatsApp in a “sponsored” slot above the real version. As reported earlier by Android Authority, the WhatsApp dupe has racked up over 500,000 downloads and, at the time of writing, its Play Store listing is still live. The WhatsApp clone is from a developer going by “Agment Assets sallu” who doesn’t currently have anything else listed on the Play Store. Their listing for the WhatsApp impostor has the same icon, screenshots, and text as the real version, but the real WhatsApp has over 10 billion downloads, an “editor’s choice” badge, and over 246 million reviews. Android Authority points out that the WhatsApp clone may be using Google Play’s Early Access program to disable public user reviews, which could have helped users warn people against downloading the app.

passages: Imagine saving up for months to buy your dream iPhone , only to discover, days later, that it is a counterfeit. It looked like the real deal, came in shiny boxes, and even the seller called it "London used" or "Grade A." But soon enough, the battery starts to die, the camera is embarrassingly out of focus, and the so-called "iOS" starts to crash like a bungling old Android phone .

This happens way too often in Nigeria, especially in popular markets like Computer Village, online platforms like Jiji, or social media. These "Made-in-China" versions look the same, from Apple's logo to the user interface, but internally, they are cheap knockoffs.

If you are going to buy an iPhone from somewhere other than an authorised Apple reseller, this article is your survival kit. It will help you spot an imitation iPhone and get a genuine one , either new, refurbished, or "UK used."

There is a huge demand for Apple products, and they come with hefty price tags. Everyone wants an iPhone, but not everyone can afford to purchase a new one from official dealers. That mismatch has created a massive market for counterfeits, phones made in China that look exactly like the real thing but have entirely different internal hardware, software, and performance.

These fake iPhones are diverse; some even have fake iOS interfaces, Apple logos, and realistic packaging. But no matter how sophisticated they may look, they usually have poor performance, bad cameras, and no ability to support future software updates. Buttons: The power button, volume, and mute switch must be responsive and firm. In clones, these are soft or loose.
Font and Spacing: Check the "iPhone" marking on the back closely. The font and spacing in counterfeit models are usually incorrect.
Camera Placement: Most fake iPhone cameras are off-centre or not flush with the surface.

App Store: Tap on the "App Store" icon. If it takes you to the Google Play Store, it's a fake.
Smoothness: iOS animations are smooth and consistent. Fake iPhones lag, especially when switching apps or opening the camera.
Settings Menu: Apple's setting aesthetic is unique and minimalistic. If you notice an "About Phone" section or any other Android-like features, that's your proof.
Every iPhone has an IMEI (International Mobile Equipment Identity) number. You can obtain this by calling *#06# on the device or going to Settings > General > About.
Obtain the IMEI or serial number, then go to Apple's Check Coverage page. Enter the number. If you receive "Invalid" or "Not Found," you have a clone.
This is one of the most certain ways to check for authenticity.
Only real iPhones can access iCloud and FaceTime. If you try to sign into an Apple ID and the phone keeps giving you errors or redirecting you somewhere strange, it's a clone.
Also, try activating Find My iPhone or FaceTime. If these options are missing or don’t work, you’ve got a fake on your hands.

Apple uses a Lightning connector, which is very specific in design. Some fake iPhones come with micro-USB or USB-C charging ports. Even if they appear to have Lightning, inserting a genuine Apple cable often feels loose or doesn't work.
One of the simplest checks? Just say, “Hey, Siri.” Real iPhones will respond instantly. Most fakes can’t replicate this correctly or at all.
If Siri doesn’t activate or behave abnormally, chances are you’re holding a fake iPhone.

Accessories appearing generic or not like those included by Apple
Even the plastic wrapping on an original iPhone is high quality and tightly wrapped. On clones, it's loose or poorly sealed.

Some sellers will try to sell you a sealed box and tell you it's "new." Don't trust them. Always have them turn on the phone before you pay. Most counterfeit iPhones are sold in sealed boxes that appear original but contain substandard phones inside.
If the seller is unwilling to open the box or gives you some excuse like "You can't return it after unboxing," walk away.

The slightly additional expense is worth the peace of mind.

sources.title: Israeli spyware targeted 'hundreds of millions' through zero-click ads, researchers find - Middle East Eye
passages: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation .

Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report.
Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021.
The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday.
The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network.
ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict".

Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it.
The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020.
