extraction.body: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation . The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday. The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network. Mercenary spyware is a highly advanced, custom-built form of malware created by private companies and sold to paying clients, including states. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report. The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it. During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy. Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US. Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe. Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others. Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021. The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021. ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict". Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market. sources.title: How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk - Al Jazeera
passages: An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat.
“We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru.

The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024.
Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance.
“Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part.
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets.

Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.

In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

extraction.body: A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part. Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything. An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims. In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files. An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks. Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera. “This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.” Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners. Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries. Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable. Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera. “To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities. “The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said. Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time. Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect. While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection. Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on. “Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.” “Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added. Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax. In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse. Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found. The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat. Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab. In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.” The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said. Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

“The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said.

Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials.

It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time.
Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect.
While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection.

Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on.

“Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
“Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added.

Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax.
In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse.

Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found.

The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat.

Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab.

In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.”

The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said.

Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

extraction.body: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation . The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday. The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network. Mercenary spyware is a highly advanced, custom-built form of malware created by private companies and sold to paying clients, including states. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report. The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it. During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy. Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US. Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe. Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others. Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021. The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021. ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict". Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market. passages: An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat.
“We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru.

The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024.
Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance.
“Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part.
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets.

Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.

In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files. An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks. Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera. “This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.” Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners. Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries. Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable. Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera. “To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities. “The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said. Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time. Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect. While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection. Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on. “Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.” “Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added. Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax. In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse. Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found. The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat. Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab. In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.” The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said. Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

passages: While Kessel Run partnered with Pivotal Labs for training to get off the ground, using military personnel offers several critical advantages.
First, doing so helps to develop products too small for current contracting systems.
These “minor” gaps range from individual mission planning applications, like the tanker fueler app, to connecting databases or reporting systems to enhance communication between operational units.
At present, servicemembers must overcome these technical problems with laborious and often inaccurate work streams, wasting time and money.
Done well, outcome products can achieve immediate operational impact and scale across the force— like the $13 million and 1,100 man-hours Kessel Run saves the Air Force each month.
Second, utilizing military personnel accelerates code delivery.
Even if a contractor is available, the project is well understood, and developers have the relevant context to solve problems, success is uncertain and can take months to deploy solutions.
This exposes servicemembers to risks and vulnerabilities during combat operations, even when they have identified capability gaps.

While faster acquisitions can address some of these challenges, it cannot compete with Kessel Run’s responsiveness, using benchmarks like going from concept to MVP in 124 days or deploying updates to production every 11.2 hours.
We believe we have demonstrated the ability to continuously deliver software that adds value to the warfighter.”
The US military must be able to sense and respond to the adversary with new code and new algorithms faster than the adversary can develop its own.
In other words, you don’t go to war with the software you develop, you go to war with the coders you develop and they ought to be soldiers, sailors, airmen, and Marines.
Making software development into a core competency is just one example of this.
Air Force is quietly proving that software development is a warfighting enabler.
Sanders represented the customer, and without the customer’s buy-in, there was a real risk that new tools would simply be shelved rather than adopted for use.
The AOC program office had its own priorities, but after lengthy and tense negotiations, the three groups agreed to join forces.
Oti’s project, they were already recruiting and selecting airmen with interest and experience in computer science.
We recognize that countless entrepreneurs have pitched their ideas as “Uber for X” and failed to deliver the exponential returns implicit in this promise.

The team also made a crucial choice to initially focus on a specific targeting tool rather than trying to boil the ocean with an entire aerial operations system.
Less than ninety days later, the team produced its first tool and put it in the hands of real users.
Estimating the cost savings of a targeting tool is difficult—what’s the cost of a strike or a miss?
However, the tanker planning tool can count savings in planes, hours, and gallons.
This saved enough money to pay for the tool and the initial training costs within a few weeks.
By then, the team was already on to its next projects.
At the heart of the Kessel Run origin story is a clear tactical problem that needed solving—the first of many.
Across the acquisition spectrum, contractors have struggled to deliver useable products on time.
A common refrain is that the military keeps moving the goal posts as requirements change while the product is in a development pipeline or a year or longer.
The articles and other content which appear on the Modern War Institute website are unofficial expressions of opinion.
The views expressed are those of the authors, and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, Department of the Army, or Department of Defense.
In broader economic terms, this is a classic make-or-buy problem.
The military needs to start making more software, just as it “makes” much of its logistics, maintenance, medical, and even religious products and services.
In-sourcing software development also protects against disruptions from civilian contractors.
Third, a process that leverages uniformed personnel helps shape the development of the next generation of military leadership.
Preparing for multi-domain operations requires the Pentagon to develop today’s emerging leaders with the technical experience necessary to navigate a digital battlefield.
Internal software development teams can address this challenge by providing experience running teams with digital tools.

Kessel Run learned not only that was it possible to develop such talent, but that it was critical that coders and designers were complemented by leaders that could manage technical projects to create operational capabilities.

It is very likely that such resistance stems from a lack of understanding about these skills’ centrality to modern operations and how lessons from Kessel Run can propel the Pentagon’s modernization efforts.

As an example, if you’ve never built a car before, you’d be well served to first try to build something that can drive—a go-kart, not a Ferrari.

extraction.body: The US. Air Force is quietly proving that software development is a warfighting enabler. Kessel Run , the Air Force’s “software factory,” is a testament to what happens when you empower servicemembers to innovate and build their own tools. Growing from concept to two thousand airmen, government civilians, and contractors in three years, Kessel Run and its offspring have saved millions of dollars while improving mission effectiveness and established best practices for military software development. While there have been calls for military software developers for years, the Air Force’s sister services are watching and are now considering whether and how to create similar software and product development teams. This is a significant organizational change and critics have pointed to challenges in developing cyber and space capabilities that could similarly affect software development efforts—that it might have the same difficulty in recruiting and retaining talent that currently plagues the cyber community, for example, or that billet structures and career advancement will be uncertain for these personnel. On an esoteric level, there is less agreement on whether software development needs to be in uniform since it is a capability rather than a new warfighting domain (as space and cyber are). But the evidence from the Air Force’s experience is clear: uniformed software developers deliver products that are higher-quality and more useful than those from traditional contractors. Further, the ubiquitous nature of software on the digital battlefield requires military leaders to see Kessel Run as a proof of concept that should be scaled across the services, instead of treating it as an isolated initiative. We recognize that countless entrepreneurs have pitched their ideas as “Uber for X” and failed to deliver the exponential returns implicit in this promise. Duplicating the success of Kessel Run in other services will require more than just the basic ingredients: money, offices, laptops, and people. The real story of Kessel Run is one of good timing, the right people, fortuitous connections, and excellent branding. Learning from the Air Force’s Kessel Run experience provides insights for minimizing risk and maximizing servicemember impact while scaling this capability across the military. In late 2016, Air Force Col. Enrique Oti began standing up a team at the Defense Innovation Unit-Experimental (DIUx) in California to develop a command-and-control planning tool. A few months later, in 2017, the Defense Innovation Board toured the Central Command Air Operations Center in Qatar to study how technology was being leveraged to fight the Islamic State. During this visit, board members, including Eric Schmidt, the executive chairman of Google’s parent company , were shocked to see soldiers and airmen manually transcribing data from one digital system into another, inviting human error and inefficient workflows. More unbelievable, they saw Air Force personnel planning air fueler flight missions on white boards, spending hours each day on a process that was creating suboptimal results while being vulnerable to everything from changes in mission planning to simply being erased accidentally. The board members could not square these observations with the notion that this was the world’s premier twenty-first-century military. The US military had been conducting combat operations in the region for a decade and a half and the annual costs of these inaccuracies totaling over a hundred million dollars of wasted fuel and constrained mission capability—not to mention the cost of the people doing the work. Additionally, Northtrop Grumman was years behind schedule and millions of dollars over budget in delivering a contract intended to modernize air operations centers. Almost immediately, the DIUx director called Col. Oti and told him to pivot to the tanker planning tool. During his deployment, as a multi-million-dollar drone tracked the enemy ground vehicles, Capt. Kroger used Google Earth to estimate distance and then crudely time the vehicle’s drive between known points to estimate vehicle speed while also estimating the weapon’s time of flight, drone flight speed, and impact location. This mismatch between sophisticated weapons and unsophisticated planning tools risked any number of problematic outcomes, from civilian casualties to operational failure. Moreover, it was unnecessary: the drone was able to pinpoint the location of the vehicle using its GPS and sensors, but no one had added the additional algorithm to estimate the vehicle’s speed, even though this is required data for an engagement. No one was talking to the users and Capt. Kroger wanted to fix that while modernizing the suite of tools. In April 2017, Col. Oti, Capt. Kroger, and Lt. Col. Jeremiah Sanders, from the Air Force Air Operations Center (AOC) program office, got approval to stand up an Air Force software development team. In a way, Lt. Col. Sanders represented the customer, and without the customer’s buy-in, there was a real risk that new tools would simply be shelved rather than adopted for use. The AOC program office had its own priorities, but after lengthy and tense negotiations, the three groups agreed to join forces. Under Col. Oti’s project, they were already recruiting and selecting airmen with interest and experience in computer science. Kessel Run partnered with Pivotal Labs to train the airmen and later settled in office space from WeWork through an office management service contract. The team also made a crucial choice to initially focus on a specific targeting tool rather than trying to boil the ocean with an entire aerial operations system. Less than ninety days later, the team produced its first tool and put it in the hands of real users. Estimating the cost savings of a targeting tool is difficult—what’s the cost of a strike or a miss? However, the tanker planning tool can count savings in planes, hours, and gallons. The tool went live in March 2017 (prior to Kessel Run’s official launch) and immediately improved planning efficiency, allowing the Air Force to use fewer aircraft each day. This saved enough money to pay for the tool and the initial training costs within a few weeks. By then, the team was already on to its next projects. Lesson 1: Think big, start small, then scale. While there have been calls for military software developers for years, the Air Force’s sister services are watching and are now considering whether and how to create similar software and product development teams. This is a significant organizational change and critics have pointed to challenges in developing cyber and space capabilities that could similarly affect software development efforts—that it might have the same difficulty in recruiting and retaining talent that currently plagues the cyber community, for example, or that billet structures and career advancement will be uncertain for these personnel. On an esoteric level, there is less agreement on whether software development needs to be in uniform since it is a capability rather than a new warfighting domain (as space and cyber are).

But the evidence from the Air Force’s experience is clear: uniformed software developers deliver products that are higher-quality and more useful than those from traditional contractors. Further, the ubiquitous nature of software on the digital battlefield requires military leaders to see Kessel Run as a proof of concept that should be scaled across the services, instead of treating it as an isolated initiative.

We recognize that countless entrepreneurs have pitched their ideas as “Uber for X” and failed to deliver the exponential returns implicit in this promise. The board members could not square these observations with the notion that this was the world’s premier twenty-first-century military. Almost immediately, the DIUx director called Col. Oti and told him to pivot to the tanker planning tool.

Moreover, it was unnecessary: the drone was able to pinpoint the location of the vehicle using its GPS and sensors, but no one had added the additional algorithm to estimate the vehicle’s speed, even though this is required data for an engagement. No one was talking to the users and Capt. Kroger wanted to fix that while modernizing the suite of tools.

passages: Almost a decade ago, the Air Force created Kessel Run in 2017 as a military-commercial partnership and Airmen-led “software factory” in response to the service’s troubled rollout of the Air Operations Center 10.2.
Viola sat down recently with Air & Space Forces Magazine to talk about where Kessel Run has been and where it’s headed.
A: I would not say that Kessel Run’s mission has changed at all.
Our mission is to deliver the AOC weapons system.
What does that look like in a software-defined future?
How do we iteratively deliver capability in that space?
Most notably is the pivot from organic, software delivery, blue-suited developers doing code to a contractor-led model today.
A: I think there are two places where AI is very applicable.
One is accelerating capability production, capability delivery, and partnering with the defense industrial base.
And the other place is: how do you integrate that into operations?
If somebody has a new capability, I’m not going to turn a blind eye.
A: If you rewind five to eight years, the acquisition transformation has also drastically changed the landscape.

Viola has spent his career at the Air Force Research Laboratory, National Security Agency, and the Idaho National Laboratory, and previously served as commander of the 346th Test Squadron at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, which runs independent operational testing and evaluation of cyber capabilities. He also served as the inaugural leader of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s “Platform One,” also based in San Antonio, the Department of the Air Force entity that provides Development, Security, and Operations as a service. Viola sat down recently with Air & Space Forces Magazine to talk about where Kessel Run has been and where it’s headed. A: I would not say that Kessel Run’s mission has changed at all. But as far as organic delivery for Kessel Run, we’re no longer a software factory. Our mission is to deliver the AOC weapons system. What does that look like in a software-defined future? How do we iteratively deliver capability in that space? Kessel Run has had several transitions. Most notably is the pivot from organic, software delivery, blue-suited developers doing code to a contractor-led model today. Q: What changed that led to this transition? A: If you rewind five to eight years, the acquisition transformation has also drastically changed the landscape. Technology has changed as well. In a previous job at Platform One, we were standing up the first really [Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery] pipeline within the Department of Defense to deliver software at speed. Industry has kind of latched onto that. That’s a commodity these days. There are vendors downstairs; you could just go buy a platform today. You could kind of even see that in cloud space over the past, you know, eight to 10 years, where you had [Defense Information System Agency], private clouds. Now you can just go purchase that as a commodity. I think from a Kessel Run standpoint, what we’ve really done is we’ve just changed to adapt to the current landscape. A: I’m in the planning stages of going to check out an airline’s global operations center. I don’t know whether the answer is that industry already does what AOCs do, or whether airlines do that, but they manage tens of thousands of flights a day. They deal with weather around the globe. They deal with pilots and flight attendants who get sick. They have a snowstorm and have to optimize for tomorrow by repositioning their aircraft in the right places. A: I think there are two places where AI is very applicable. One is accelerating capability production, capability delivery, and partnering with the defense industrial base. What can we leverage, and then how do we apply it to the problem set? If somebody has a new capability, I’m not going to turn a blind eye. What we’re trying to do is drive synergies across that space. While we’re trying to do aircrew readiness, and that in itself is a problem to solve, we are also keeping an eye on how we operate in a dynamic environment, not just on day-to-day operations, which is dynamic enough, but also in wartime operations, and trying to pull those two together. Almost a decade ago, the Air Force created Kessel Run in 2017 as a military-commercial partnership and Airmen-led “software factory” in response to the service’s troubled rollout of the Air Operations Center 10.2.

The program scored early wins with “Jigsaw,” a cloud-based tanker aircraft planning application, and spawned a network of software factories across the Air Force. NATO adopted Jigsaw in 2020, and planners used the first cloud-generated Air Tasking Order via the Kessel Run All Domain Operations Suite, KRADOS. Personnel also injected real-time software updates for command-and-control work during the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021.
A month later, Kessel Run signed a formal user agreement with Air Combat Command that put the fledgling but successful organization into the Pentagon’s software acquisition pathway.

Then, in 2025, Kessel Run shifted from its small teams of Active-duty Coders to a “government-led, vendor-managed” model. This February , KR kicked off its most ambitious efforts yet under the new model, an effort to create the “next generation” of the Air Operations Centers that integrate artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data fusion.

Col. Brian Viola took the helm at Kessel Run in June and is now charged with taking the baton from past leaders while sprinting ahead as the Air Force seeks a modernized AOC to serve as the key nodes in its updated command and control network.

Viola has spent his career at the Air Force Research Laboratory, National Security Agency, and the Idaho National Laboratory, and previously served as commander of the 346th Test Squadron at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, which runs independent operational testing and evaluation of cyber capabilities. He also served as the inaugural leader of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s “Platform One,” also based in San Antonio, the Department of the Air Force entity that provides Development, Security, and Operations as a service.
Viola sat down recently with Air & Space Forces Magazine to talk about where Kessel Run has been and where it’s headed.

What does that look like in a software-defined future? How do we iteratively deliver capability in that space? Kessel Run has had several transitions. Most notably is the pivot from organic, software delivery, blue-suited developers doing code to a contractor-led model today.

Q: What changed that led to this transition? A: If you rewind five to eight years, the acquisition transformation has also drastically changed the landscape. Technology has changed as well. In a previous job at Platform One, we were standing up the first really [Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery] pipeline within the Department of Defense to deliver software at speed. Industry has kind of latched onto that. That’s a commodity these days. There are vendors downstairs; you could just go buy a platform today. You could kind of even see that in cloud space over the past, you know, eight to 10 years, where you had [Defense Information System Agency], private clouds. Now you can just go purchase that as a commodity. I think from a Kessel Run standpoint, what we’ve really done is we’ve just changed to adapt to the current landscape.
Q: With modernizing the AOC, are there other partners, allies, industry or commercial operations that USAF can draw on for ideas?

A: I’m in the planning stages of going to check out an airline’s global operations center. I don’t know whether the answer is that industry already does what AOCs do, or whether airlines do that, but they manage tens of thousands of flights a day. They deal with weather around the globe. They deal with pilots and flight attendants who get sick. They have a snowstorm and have to optimize for tomorrow by repositioning their aircraft in the right places. They’re optimizing for fuel costs and passengers. The real question that I have is: are the tools to do that and [the tools] the AOC needs drastically different? Can we use the same algorithms with different weights to optimize for different things?
Q: How does AI fit into what Kessel Run is trying to do with the AOCs?

A: I think there are two places where AI is very applicable. One is accelerating capability production, capability delivery, and partnering with the defense industrial base. We can leverage that smartly. And the other place is: how do you integrate that into operations? We’re in constant conversation with the AOC commanders, with [Air Combat Command], and even at the Department of the Air Force level on what’s available. What is enterprise-level? What can we leverage, and then how do we apply it to the problem set? If somebody has a new capability, I’m not going to turn a blind eye. If the Department of War has a capability we can leverage against a problem set, then I think Kessel Run has the right culture to push boundaries where needed to deliver that capability to the warfighter.

Q: The Air Force recently announced that Kessel Run had partnered with Air Combat Command and Air Education and Training Command on the Aerospace Readiness Enterprise System aimed at aircrew readiness. What should we know about ARES and how it relates to AOC modernization?

A: Where I find it very interesting is when you look at that problem set of aircrew readiness through a larger lens that includes the AOC, fully acknowledging that aircrew readiness during peacetime looks one way, and another during war, but many of the fundamentals remain during times of war. For instance, you need to have crew rest. You need to be able to turn maintenance on platforms. People need to be certified. You need to get people in and out of theater. coreStoryFacts.text: While Kessel Run partnered with Pivotal Labs for training to get off the ground, using military personnel offers several critical advantages.
First, doing so helps to develop products too small for current contracting systems.
These “minor” gaps range from individual mission planning applications, like the tanker fueler app, to connecting databases or reporting systems to enhance communication between operational units.
At present, servicemembers must overcome these technical problems with laborious and often inaccurate work streams, wasting time and money.
Done well, outcome products can achieve immediate operational impact and scale across the force— like the $13 million and 1,100 man-hours Kessel Run saves the Air Force each month.
Second, utilizing military personnel accelerates code delivery.
Even if a contractor is available, the project is well understood, and developers have the relevant context to solve problems, success is uncertain and can take months to deploy solutions.
This exposes servicemembers to risks and vulnerabilities during combat operations, even when they have identified capability gaps.

While faster acquisitions can address some of these challenges, it cannot compete with Kessel Run’s responsiveness, using benchmarks like going from concept to MVP in 124 days or deploying updates to production every 11.2 hours.
We believe we have demonstrated the ability to continuously deliver software that adds value to the warfighter.”
The US military must be able to sense and respond to the adversary with new code and new algorithms faster than the adversary can develop its own.
In other words, you don’t go to war with the software you develop, you go to war with the coders you develop and they ought to be soldiers, sailors, airmen, and Marines.
Making software development into a core competency is just one example of this.
Air Force is quietly proving that software development is a warfighting enabler.
Sanders represented the customer, and without the customer’s buy-in, there was a real risk that new tools would simply be shelved rather than adopted for use.
The AOC program office had its own priorities, but after lengthy and tense negotiations, the three groups agreed to join forces.
Oti’s project, they were already recruiting and selecting airmen with interest and experience in computer science.
We recognize that countless entrepreneurs have pitched their ideas as “Uber for X” and failed to deliver the exponential returns implicit in this promise.
Duplicating the success of Kessel Run in other services will require more than just the basic ingredients: money, offices, laptops, and people.
The team also made a crucial choice to initially focus on a specific targeting tool rather than trying to boil the ocean with an entire aerial operations system.
Less than ninety days later, the team produced its first tool and put it in the hands of real users.
Estimating the cost savings of a targeting tool is difficult—what’s the cost of a strike or a miss?
However, the tanker planning tool can count savings in planes, hours, and gallons.
This saved enough money to pay for the tool and the initial training costs within a few weeks.

extraction.body: The US. Air Force is quietly proving that software development is a warfighting enabler. Kessel Run , the Air Force’s “software factory,” is a testament to what happens when you empower servicemembers to innovate and build their own tools. Growing from concept to two thousand airmen, government civilians, and contractors in three years, Kessel Run and its offspring have saved millions of dollars while improving mission effectiveness and established best practices for military software development. While there have been calls for military software developers for years, the Air Force’s sister services are watching and are now considering whether and how to create similar software and product development teams. This is a significant organizational change and critics have pointed to challenges in developing cyber and space capabilities that could similarly affect software development efforts—that it might have the same difficulty in recruiting and retaining talent that currently plagues the cyber community, for example, or that billet structures and career advancement will be uncertain for these personnel. On an esoteric level, there is less agreement on whether software development needs to be in uniform since it is a capability rather than a new warfighting domain (as space and cyber are). But the evidence from the Air Force’s experience is clear: uniformed software developers deliver products that are higher-quality and more useful than those from traditional contractors. Further, the ubiquitous nature of software on the digital battlefield requires military leaders to see Kessel Run as a proof of concept that should be scaled across the services, instead of treating it as an isolated initiative. We recognize that countless entrepreneurs have pitched their ideas as “Uber for X” and failed to deliver the exponential returns implicit in this promise. Duplicating the success of Kessel Run in other services will require more than just the basic ingredients: money, offices, laptops, and people. The real story of Kessel Run is one of good timing, the right people, fortuitous connections, and excellent branding. Learning from the Air Force’s Kessel Run experience provides insights for minimizing risk and maximizing servicemember impact while scaling this capability across the military. In late 2016, Air Force Col. Enrique Oti began standing up a team at the Defense Innovation Unit-Experimental (DIUx) in California to develop a command-and-control planning tool. A few months later, in 2017, the Defense Innovation Board toured the Central Command Air Operations Center in Qatar to study how technology was being leveraged to fight the Islamic State. During this visit, board members, including Eric Schmidt, the executive chairman of Google’s parent company , were shocked to see soldiers and airmen manually transcribing data from one digital system into another, inviting human error and inefficient workflows. More unbelievable, they saw Air Force personnel planning air fueler flight missions on white boards, spending hours each day on a process that was creating suboptimal results while being vulnerable to everything from changes in mission planning to simply being erased accidentally. The board members could not square these observations with the notion that this was the world’s premier twenty-first-century military. The US military had been conducting combat operations in the region for a decade and a half and the annual costs of these inaccuracies totaling over a hundred million dollars of wasted fuel and constrained mission capability—not to mention the cost of the people doing the work. Additionally, Northtrop Grumman was years behind schedule and millions of dollars over budget in delivering a contract intended to modernize air operations centers. Almost immediately, the DIUx director called Col. Oti and told him to pivot to the tanker planning tool. During his deployment, as a multi-million-dollar drone tracked the enemy ground vehicles, Capt. Kroger used Google Earth to estimate distance and then crudely time the vehicle’s drive between known points to estimate vehicle speed while also estimating the weapon’s time of flight, drone flight speed, and impact location. This mismatch between sophisticated weapons and unsophisticated planning tools risked any number of problematic outcomes, from civilian casualties to operational failure. Moreover, it was unnecessary: the drone was able to pinpoint the location of the vehicle using its GPS and sensors, but no one had added the additional algorithm to estimate the vehicle’s speed, even though this is required data for an engagement. No one was talking to the users and Capt. Kroger wanted to fix that while modernizing the suite of tools. In April 2017, Col. Oti, Capt. Kroger, and Lt. Col. Jeremiah Sanders, from the Air Force Air Operations Center (AOC) program office, got approval to stand up an Air Force software development team. In a way, Lt. Col. Sanders represented the customer, and without the customer’s buy-in, there was a real risk that new tools would simply be shelved rather than adopted for use. The AOC program office had its own priorities, but after lengthy and tense negotiations, the three groups agreed to join forces. Under Col. Oti’s project, they were already recruiting and selecting airmen with interest and experience in computer science. Kessel Run partnered with Pivotal Labs to train the airmen and later settled in office space from WeWork through an office management service contract. The team also made a crucial choice to initially focus on a specific targeting tool rather than trying to boil the ocean with an entire aerial operations system. Less than ninety days later, the team produced its first tool and put it in the hands of real users. Estimating the cost savings of a targeting tool is difficult—what’s the cost of a strike or a miss? However, the tanker planning tool can count savings in planes, hours, and gallons. The tool went live in March 2017 (prior to Kessel Run’s official launch) and immediately improved planning efficiency, allowing the Air Force to use fewer aircraft each day. This saved enough money to pay for the tool and the initial training costs within a few weeks. By then, the team was already on to its next projects. Lesson 1: Think big, start small, then scale. Kessel Run’s journey speaks to the power of driving innovation from the tactical level with senior-leader support (and not the inverse). Entrepreneurs and technologists speak often about building a “minimum viable product,” or MVP. This is the prototype that you can put in the hands of a user to begin iterative refinement of design and functionality. As an example, if you’ve never built a car before, you’d be well served to first try to build something that can drive—a go-kart, not a Ferrari. In the context of Kessel Run, both the organization and its products leveraged this model: start small, refine, and scale. Looking at the organization, instead of establishing a three-thousand-airman software wing, the program began with a very small team, demonstrated effectiveness, and has now grown based on proof of concept. This means that the organization contains only the people and resources needed for existing problems and that new teams (and processes) are created to address needs. Although this approach is initially crude, the refinement process improves quality while minimizing organizational fluff. Lesson 2: Software development is a tactical enabler. At the heart of the Kessel Run origin story is a clear tactical problem that needed solving—the first of many. Across the acquisition spectrum, contractors have struggled to deliver useable products on time. A common refrain is that the military keeps moving the goal posts as requirements change while the product is in a development pipeline or a year or longer. Kessel Run was able to address this more effectively than the existing contractor by developing software using commercial industry best practices, specifically “agile” software development. In software development, “agile” is not a bastardized military buzzword. Instead, the term refers to a development methodology that uses direct customer feedback to drive development through sprints lasting one to four weeks. Readers familiar with the military’s targeting cycle will find agile software development familiar. After building an MVP, each of these sprints provides value to customers by releasing new code and building the next development iteration around emerging customer needs. In a military context, agile development has two unique challenges: the users are frequently deployed and their feedback requires understanding a workflow that lacks a civilian equivalent. Agile development differs from traditional acquisition approaches since constant feedback loops decrease risk of making the wrong product and the approach focuses on creating immediate customer value. Continuing the car analogy, the “waterfall” method would have independent teams building the engine, frame, wheels, and seats in isolation with a major milestone only coming when the teams test putting them together at the end of the year. Agile development avoids this problem. (Recognizing the challenges of changing industry processes, the Defense Innovation Board has even published a Guide to Detecting Agile BS .) In broader economic terms, this is a classic make-or-buy problem. The military needs to start making more software, just as it “makes” much of its logistics, maintenance, medical, and even religious products and services. In-sourcing software development also protects against disruptions from civilian contractors. In an extreme example, Google declined to renew its Project Maven contract after employee backlash surrounding the Department of Defense drone project. While we recognize the difference between cutting-edge machine-learning projects and the sort of back-office or productivity tools that Kessel Run’s embedded software developers are creating, the lesson is no less relevant: the competition for digital talent may prevent the Pentagon from ready access to the key enablers needed for time-sensitive capability gaps. One of the most effective strategies for mitigating these market sensitivities are upskilling campaigns using internal personnel. At one time, basic electronics were a subject for research labs, but the services now have electricians (and even nuclear technicians). On an esoteric level, there is less agreement on whether software development needs to be in uniform since it is a capability rather than a new warfighting domain (as space and cyber are).

Further, the ubiquitous nature of software on the digital battlefield requires military leaders to see Kessel Run as a proof of concept that should be scaled across the services, instead of treating it as an isolated initiative.

We recognize that countless entrepreneurs have pitched their ideas as “Uber for X” and failed to deliver the exponential returns implicit in this promise. Duplicating the success of Kessel Run in other services will require more than just the basic ingredients: money, offices, laptops, and people. Almost immediately, the DIUx director called Col. Oti and told him to pivot to the tanker planning tool.

Kroger used Google Earth to estimate distance and then crudely time the vehicle’s drive between known points to estimate vehicle speed while also estimating the weapon’s time of flight, drone flight speed, and impact location. This mismatch between sophisticated weapons and unsophisticated planning tools risked any number of problematic outcomes, from civilian casualties to operational failure. Moreover, it was unnecessary: the drone was able to pinpoint the location of the vehicle using its GPS and sensors, but no one had added the additional algorithm to estimate the vehicle’s speed, even though this is required data for an engagement. No one was talking to the users and Capt. Kroger wanted to fix that while modernizing the suite of tools.

sources.title: Q&A: No Longer a Software Factory, What’s Next for Air Force’s Kessel Run? - Air & Space Forces Magazine
passages: Almost a decade ago, the Air Force created Kessel Run in 2017 as a military-commercial partnership and Airmen-led “software factory” in response to the service’s troubled rollout of the Air Operations Center 10.2.
Viola sat down recently with Air & Space Forces Magazine to talk about where Kessel Run has been and where it’s headed.
A: I would not say that Kessel Run’s mission has changed at all.
Our mission is to deliver the AOC weapons system.
What does that look like in a software-defined future?
How do we iteratively deliver capability in that space?
Most notably is the pivot from organic, software delivery, blue-suited developers doing code to a contractor-led model today.
A: I think there are two places where AI is very applicable.
One is accelerating capability production, capability delivery, and partnering with the defense industrial base.
And the other place is: how do you integrate that into operations?
If somebody has a new capability, I’m not going to turn a blind eye.
A: If you rewind five to eight years, the acquisition transformation has also drastically changed the landscape.
In a previous job at Platform One, we were standing up the first really [Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery] pipeline within the Department of Defense to deliver software at speed.
There are vendors downstairs; you could just go buy a platform today.
You could kind of even see that in cloud space over the past, you know, eight to 10 years, where you had [Defense Information System Agency], private clouds.
Now you can just go purchase that as a commodity.
Then, in 2025, Kessel Run shifted from its small teams of Active-duty Coders to a “government-led, vendor-managed” model.
What should we know about ARES and how it relates to AOC modernization?

Find out more at afa.org Almost a decade ago, the Air Force created Kessel Run in 2017 as a military-commercial partnership and Airmen-led “software factory” in response to the service’s troubled rollout of the Air Operations Center 10.2. The name, a nod to the Star Wars movie franchise, references a smuggling route that hero Han Solo bragged about making in “12 parsecs.” It also served as a reminder for Airmen coders to move fast and overcome complex software demands under intense pressure and tight timelines through bureaucratic obstacles, much like the space monsters, asteroids, gravity distortions, and stellar anomalies that often doomed pilots attempting to make the Kessel Run. sources.title: a16z’s Aerie Targets a Key Bottleneck in Post-Quantum Blockchain Design - The Crypto Times
passages: A separate proposal covered by The Crypto Times on October 14 explores how Bitcoin transactions could use post-quantum cryptography while limiting the amount of data stored on-chain .
The proposal uses a mechanism called a degriefer to distinguish legitimate transactions from conflicting spends.
Its stated goal is to reduce on-chain data storage, with a proposed transaction size of 96 bytes.
a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler and co-authors have introduced Aerie, a proof system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single proof.

The research addresses a challenge for proof-of-stake blockchains exploring quantum-resistant cryptography : post-quantum signatures are generally larger than current signatures and cannot be aggregated using the same method as Ethereum ’s BLS signatures.
The paper identifies Falcon as one option for post-quantum blockchain applications.
Thaler argued that lattice-based cryptography should remain under consideration as blockchains develop post-quantum systems.
He said lattice-based proofs could reduce reliance on recursive proofs and custom hash-based signatures.
BLS signatures rely on elliptic-curve cryptography, which is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures.
The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort.
It also discloses that Thaler is an investor in blockchain-based platforms through a16z.
Further evaluation will be needed to assess Aerie’s suitability for distributed blockchain consensus.
These constraints mean that proving speed alone does not establish whether Aerie is suitable for replacing existing aggregation systems in blockchain consensus.
Changes to the final standard could affect aspects of Aerie’s design, including message hashing.
Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a lattice-based proof system.
