extraction.body: Aerie aggregates 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds on an Apple M4 Max, with the authors reporting smaller proofs and faster verification. a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler and co-authors have introduced Aerie, a proof system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single proof. In an October 16 thread on X, Thaler said Aerie aggregated 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds on an Apple M4 Max laptop CPU. The research addresses a challenge for proof-of-stake blockchains exploring quantum-resistant cryptography : post-quantum signatures are generally larger than current signatures and cannot be aggregated using the same method as Ethereum ’s BLS signatures. 1/ Today we’re releasing Aerie: fast post-quantum signature aggregation , using lattice-based SNARKs for lattice-based Falcon signatures. On a laptop (CPU only), it aggregates roughly a full Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures (32,768) in 0.65 seconds. The team published a research paper hosted by LayerZero Labs and released the implementation code on GitHub. Proof-of-stake blockchains use digital signatures to verify validator participation. Ethereum aggregates validator BLS signatures into a single signature for each slot, reducing the data required to verify participation. BLS signatures rely on elliptic-curve cryptography, which is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Post-quantum signature schemes are designed to resist such attacks, but their larger signatures can increase bandwidth requirements and verification costs. The paper identifies Falcon as one option for post-quantum blockchain applications. A Falcon-512 signature occupies 666 bytes, compared with approximately 64 bytes for the elliptic-curve signatures commonly used today. Without an effective aggregation method, including large numbers of post-quantum signatures in blockchain blocks could increase data requirements and the costs of operating a node . Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a lattice-based proof system. This differs from approaches that use hash-based signatures and hash-based proofs, including the approach associated with Ethereum’s leanVM. According to Thaler’s X thread , Aerie uses Akita, a lattice-based commitment scheme developed with LayerZero Labs, alongside sum-check proving techniques associated with Lattice Jolt. Thaler said hash-based signatures can require hundreds of hash calculations to verify, making them expensive to prove within a zero-knowledge proof system. Falcon’s verification process involves less hashing, allowing Aerie’s verifier to calculate message hashes directly using a short salt attached to each signature. According to the authors, this allows Aerie to prove the remaining algebraic checks without proving the hash computations. Unlike some alternative systems, Aerie does not use recursive proof merging. The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures. For Falcon-1024, a stronger parameter variant, the authors report aggregating 16,384 signatures in 0.63 seconds, with a 29-fold reduction in size. The researchers also compared Aerie with Ethereum’s leanVM approach and Orthus, a previous Falcon signature aggregator . Their reported results include: The authors said Orthus does not prove every requirement of the Falcon specification, including its byte-format rules. This qualification matters when interpreting the comparison. The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort. These results come from the researchers’ own tests and have not been independently reproduced. Performance comparisons depend on the hardware, configurations, and workloads used. Aerie’s design has trade-offs. Its prover must hold all signatures in a batch, and separate Aerie proofs cannot currently be merged. This limits its use in networks that collect signatures across multiple machines. Recursive systems such as leanVM can distribute work across machines and combine proofs into a final proof. The paper reports that Aerie’s verification takes approximately 54 milliseconds on one CPU core, compared with about 6 milliseconds for leanVM in the authors’ comparison. Proving a batch of 32,768 signatures required approximately 2.1 GiB of peak memory. The short public salts account for most of the aggregate’s size. According to the paper, using one shared salt could reduce the aggregate from approximately 1.3 MiB to 66 KiB, but that approach relies on an additional security assumption the authors have not proved. These constraints mean that proving speed alone does not establish whether Aerie is suitable for replacing existing aggregation systems in blockchain consensus. Ethereum’s long-term roadmap includes replacing cryptographic components that could become vulnerable to future quantum computers. One approach under development uses hash-based signatures and leanVM, a zero-knowledge virtual machine designed to help aggregate those signatures efficiently. However, the a16z researchers argue that relying exclusively on hash-based cryptography could introduce additional computational costs and technical complexity. Thaler argued that lattice-based cryptography should remain under consideration as blockchains develop post-quantum systems. He said lattice-based proofs could reduce reliance on recursive proofs and custom hash-based signatures. He also argued that these design considerations should be weighed against the possibility of future attacks on established lattice assumptions. The researcher referred to the Ethereum Foundation ’s strawmap, which includes a hash-based layer-one approach and plans for native private transfers. He argued that public-key encryption for private transfers cannot be built from hash functions alone, so avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs would not eliminate every potential reliance on lattice cryptography. A separate proposal covered by The Crypto Times on October 14 explores how Bitcoin transactions could use post-quantum cryptography while limiting the amount of data stored on-chain . The proposal uses a mechanism called a degriefer to distinguish legitimate transactions from conflicting spends. Its stated goal is to reduce on-chain data storage, with a proposed transaction size of 96 bytes. Unlike the Bitcoin proposal, which focuses on the size of individual transactions, Aerie aggregates batches of signatures into a single proof. The authors said Aerie’s security relies on Falcon and Module-SIS, a lattice-based computational problem. They also reported that part of the system’s soundness proof was checked using the Lean 4 theorem prover. The paper discloses that AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic assisted with implementation, benchmarking, protocol development, and security proofs. The authors said they take responsibility for the paper’s accuracy. It also discloses that Thaler is an investor in blockchain-based platforms through a16z. Falcon is being standardized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology as FN-DSA. Changes to the final standard could affect aspects of Aerie’s design, including message hashing. The authors identify GPU acceleration, smaller aggregates through hidden salts, and proof merging as areas for further research. Further evaluation will be needed to assess Aerie’s suitability for distributed blockchain consensus. The proposal uses a mechanism called a degriefer to distinguish legitimate transactions from conflicting spends.
Its stated goal is to reduce on-chain data storage, with a proposed transaction size of 96 bytes.
a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler and co-authors have introduced Aerie, a proof system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single proof.

The research addresses a challenge for proof-of-stake blockchains exploring quantum-resistant cryptography : post-quantum signatures are generally larger than current signatures and cannot be aggregated using the same method as Ethereum ’s BLS signatures.
The paper identifies Falcon as one option for post-quantum blockchain applications.
Thaler argued that lattice-based cryptography should remain under consideration as blockchains develop post-quantum systems.
He said lattice-based proofs could reduce reliance on recursive proofs and custom hash-based signatures.
BLS signatures rely on elliptic-curve cryptography, which is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures.
The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort.
It also discloses that Thaler is an investor in blockchain-based platforms through a16z.
Further evaluation will be needed to assess Aerie’s suitability for distributed blockchain consensus.
These constraints mean that proving speed alone does not establish whether Aerie is suitable for replacing existing aggregation systems in blockchain consensus.
Changes to the final standard could affect aspects of Aerie’s design, including message hashing.
Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a lattice-based proof system.

Post-quantum signatures are also 10 to 100 times larger than today’s elliptic-curve signatures, so without aggregation these signatures will bloat blocks — limiting throughput and raising the cost of running a node.
That’s why today we’re releasing Aerie , which takes the opposite approach by aggregating lattice-based signatures using lattice-based SNARKs .

For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits.

Most major blockchains besides Bitcoin run on proof of stake, where validators vote on each block by signing it. Signature aggregation is what makes large validator sets practical. Ethereum uses BLS signatures, whose algebraic structure lets it combine tens of thousands of validator signatures every slot into a single group element. Solana, where validator votes have made up about three-quarters of all transactions, is adopting BLS aggregation too, as part of its Alpenglow upgrade. But as useful as BLS is, it is not post-quantum — and in fact, no known post-quantum signature scheme aggregates this way. Post-quantum signatures are also 10 to 100 times larger than today’s elliptic-curve signatures, so without aggregation these signatures will bloat blocks — limiting throughput and raising the cost of running a node. This matters as blockchains carry a growing share of the world’s payments, from stablecoin transfers to payments made by AI agents. SNARKs (Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge) fix these issues: The “aggregate signature” becomes a single succinct proof that every signature in the batch verifies. The prevailing SNARK-based approach, central to Ethereum’s roadmap, pairs hash-based signatures with hash-based SNARKs. But this approach is slow because hash-based signatures are expensive to prove: A single laptop can’t keep up with a full slot of signatures, which is one reason Ethereum’s design splits the work across many provers and recursively merges their proofs. That’s why today we’re releasing Aerie , which takes the opposite approach by aggregating lattice-based signatures using lattice-based SNARKs . Aerie supports Falcon, a lattice-based signature scheme that NIST has selected for standardization, in both its Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 variants. Aerie is fast enough that a single laptop can aggregate roughly an Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures on its own: Aerie’s speed also makes a simpler aggregation design possible. In Ethereum’s current plan, each proof from leanVM (the zkVM being developed as part of Lean Ethereum to aggregate hash-based signatures) covers only about 900 signatures. Covering a full slot therefore takes rounds of recursive merging, and each round can’t start until the previous round’s proofs arrive. The first is Akita (the lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme we built with LayerZero Labs ), together with the sum-check-based proving techniques we developed on the road to Lattice Jolt. These techniques are highly parallel and well suited to GPUs , so Aerie has plenty of room to get even faster. The second reason Aerie is fast is the relative lack of hashing in lattice signature verification. Hash-based signatures are verified by evaluating hundreds of hashes per signature. Aggregating them means proving all of those hash evaluations — and hashing is expensive to prove, typically adding over 100x overhead relative to computing the hash natively. Lattice signatures are verified differently. The core checks are algebraic, and hashing plays only a small role: a handful of hash evaluations per signature, not hundreds. Falcon takes the lack of hashing especially far. It’s a hash-and-sign scheme whose hash takes only the message and a salt as input. So if the aggregate includes each signature’s salt, the verifier can compute every hash itself, and the proof needs to cover only the algebraic checks. That’s a big part of Aerie’s speed, and why we started with Falcon. Falcon is also compact: Falcon-1024 reaches NIST’s highest security level with signatures about half the size of ML-DSA-44’s, the lowest-security ML-DSA parameter set. We’re not suggesting every blockchain adopt Falcon. Its signing algorithm is complex, and it has historically been hard to fit on hardware wallets, relying on floating-point arithmetic and tens of kilobytes of working memory. Side-channel hardening is still an active area of work. But these drawbacks are being addressed rapidly. Recent research has shown how to implement Falcon signing with fixed-point arithmetic instead of floating point, and NIST now plans to require this approach in the FN-DSA standard. A new implementation also cuts Falcon-512 signing to about 11 kB of RAM, small enough for the secure elements in hardware wallets. For both reasons, Falcon is far easier to deploy than it was even a year ago. Hardware wallets are a challenge for stateless hash-based signatures too: The SPHINCS- variants light enough for a hardware wallet take from 47 seconds to over six minutes to sign on a Ledger secure element. For chains that weigh Falcon’s trade-offs and choose it — as Solana is exploring and Algorand has deployed — Aerie offers a fast path to aggregation. We’re also working on extensions that require proving some hashing: supporting ML-DSA, whose hash depends on the signature itself; and removing Falcon’s salts from the aggregate by proving its hash inside the SNARK. Recent advances like LaBinius offer paths to proving those few hashes efficiently. And we’re extending Aerie to hybrid signatures that pair a lattice signature with an elliptic-curve-based one, an important form of defense-in-depth. These extensions may not reach 50,000 signatures per second, but we still expect plenty of headroom over the 1,000 per second Ethereum has targeted . There’s an active debate about lattice versus hash-based cryptography in blockchain design, sharpened by speculation about what AI might mean for cryptanalysis . We’ll make the full case for embracing lattices in a future post. The short version is this: No one can promise that new attacks won’t be found on lattices, or on any other cryptography. But speculative cryptanalytic risk must be weighed against the clear and present risks built into more complicated systems. As noted above, Ethereum’s planned hash-only signature aggregation design relies on SNARK recursion, with the coordination overhead, bug surface, and unestablished security that come with that approach. Hash-only designs also lean on non-standard constructions: Ethereum’s planned consensus and account signatures are custom schemes outside NIST’s standards, with the underlying hash still undecided. This limits support from hardware wallets for individual users, and from the hardware security modules and custody systems that institutions rely on. Private payments need encryption, not just signatures and proofs: Recipients must learn about the notes sent to them, viewing keys must grant read access, and encrypted mempools must hide transactions until they’re ordered. Private payments matter to cypherpunks and financial institutions alike, and Ethereum already plans for them. The Ethereum Foundation’s strawmap , a draft long-term roadmap for its base layer, lists a private L1 with shielded transfers among its five “north stars,” alongside a hash-based post-quantum L1. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, and encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, yet encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide. A classic result of Russell Impagliazzo and Steven Rudich shows that public-key encryption cannot be built from hash functions in a black-box way. The best hash-only alternative, Merkle puzzles , gives honest users only a quadratic advantage over attackers, and this is optimal : No protocol can do better when hashes are modeled as random oracles. Even advocates of hash-only designs acknowledge this. So a private Ethereum, like any chain that supports private payments, will depend on structured cryptography somewhere in its stack — and in practice, that means lattices. ML-KEM, a lattice scheme, is NIST’s primary post-quantum encryption standard and is already deployed across much of the internet . Are there workarounds? One proposed solution is to keep encrypted notes off-chain, so fewer ciphertexts sit in public forever. But this doesn’t avoid encryption: The notes must still reach their recipients encrypted, over messaging apps and other channels that are already moving to ML-KEM. And off-chain delivery has trade-offs of its own: a channel that must stay available, can observe metadata, and whose failure can leave recipients unable to find and spend their funds. For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits. So the real question isn’t whether to rely on lattices, but whether to forgo their benefits for a false sense of security. An Aerie proof is about 66 KiB, whether it covers 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures or 16,384 Falcon-1024 signatures. That’s on par with the most compact prior lattice-based approach: PSE’s benchmarks of LaBRADOR-based Falcon aggregation report about 74 KB for 10,000 signatures, though verification there takes seconds rather than milliseconds. Because Aerie’s verifier computes each signature’s hash itself, it also needs each signature’s 40-byte salt. For large batches, the salts dominate: 32,768 of them take up about 1.3 MB, versus 66 KiB for the proof. Even so, the aggregate costs only about 42 bytes per signature, 16 times smaller than Falcon-512 signatures (666 bytes) and nearly 30 times smaller than Falcon-1024 signatures (1,280 bytes). Some deployments avoid the salt cost entirely. Algorand’s deterministic Falcon makes signing deterministic, which lets it replace the random per-signature salt with a fixed value. Aggregating its signatures would need no salts at all, just the 66 KiB proof, with small changes to how Aerie handles the salt and signature encoding. Measured against Falcon itself, Aerie’s prover is also cheap : On a single core, proving takes only about 8 times as long as standard Falcon verification of the same signatures, and 1.4 times as long as signing them. Compared with Orthus , the fastest prior Falcon aggregation scheme, Aerie (on one core of the same AVX-512 server): Moreover, Aerie proves everything a standard Falcon verifier checks. Prior Falcon aggregation work did not: It left out the check that each signature is canonically encoded, so its aggregates could accept signatures that a standard Falcon verifier would reject. We also compared Aerie with leanVM , which aggregates XMSS signatures, the stateful hash-based scheme Ethereum plans to use for consensus. On the same machine, Aerie aggregates 29x as many signatures per second (about 50,800 versus 1,770). Stateful signatures like XMSS work well at the consensus layer, where each validator signs at most one message per slot, so the slot number itself can serve as the signing state. But they pose large risks at the execution layer: A user who signs from two devices, or restores a wallet from a backup, can reuse signing state and thereby let attackers forge signatures under their key. That’s why Ethereum plans a stateless hash-based scheme for account signatures. And stateless hash-based signatures are even costlier to aggregate: In leanVM’s latest published benchmarks , on the same laptop model, it aggregates them at about 820 per second, roughly 60x slower than Aerie. (The benchmarked configuration also caps each key at about 127,000 signatures; configurations that allow far more cost more at key generation but aggregate just as fast.)

In an October 16 thread on X, Thaler said Aerie aggregated 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds on an Apple M4 Max laptop CPU. The research addresses a challenge for proof-of-stake blockchains exploring quantum-resistant cryptography : post-quantum signatures are generally larger than current signatures and cannot be aggregated using the same method as Ethereum ’s BLS signatures. 1/ Today we’re releasing Aerie: fast post-quantum signature aggregation , using lattice-based SNARKs for lattice-based Falcon signatures. On a laptop (CPU only), it aggregates roughly a full Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures (32,768) in 0.65 seconds. The team published a research paper hosted by LayerZero Labs and released the implementation code on GitHub. Proof-of-stake blockchains use digital signatures to verify validator participation. Ethereum aggregates validator BLS signatures into a single signature for each slot, reducing the data required to verify participation. BLS signatures rely on elliptic-curve cryptography, which is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Post-quantum signature schemes are designed to resist such attacks, but their larger signatures can increase bandwidth requirements and verification costs. The paper identifies Falcon as one option for post-quantum blockchain applications. A Falcon-512 signature occupies 666 bytes, compared with approximately 64 bytes for the elliptic-curve signatures commonly used today. Without an effective aggregation method, including large numbers of post-quantum signatures in blockchain blocks could increase data requirements and the costs of operating a node . Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a lattice-based proof system. This differs from approaches that use hash-based signatures and hash-based proofs, including the approach associated with Ethereum’s leanVM. According to Thaler’s X thread , Aerie uses Akita, a lattice-based commitment scheme developed with LayerZero Labs, alongside sum-check proving techniques associated with Lattice Jolt. Thaler said hash-based signatures can require hundreds of hash calculations to verify, making them expensive to prove within a zero-knowledge proof system. Falcon’s verification process involves less hashing, allowing Aerie’s verifier to calculate message hashes directly using a short salt attached to each signature. According to the authors, this allows Aerie to prove the remaining algebraic checks without proving the hash computations. Unlike some alternative systems, Aerie does not use recursive proof merging. The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures. For Falcon-1024, a stronger parameter variant, the authors report aggregating 16,384 signatures in 0.63 seconds, with a 29-fold reduction in size. The researchers also compared Aerie with Ethereum’s leanVM approach and Orthus, a previous Falcon signature aggregator . Their reported results include: The authors said Orthus does not prove every requirement of the Falcon specification, including its byte-format rules. This qualification matters when interpreting the comparison. The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort. These results come from the researchers’ own tests and have not been independently reproduced. Performance comparisons depend on the hardware, configurations, and workloads used. Aerie’s design has trade-offs. Its prover must hold all signatures in a batch, and separate Aerie proofs cannot currently be merged. This limits its use in networks that collect signatures across multiple machines. Recursive systems such as leanVM can distribute work across machines and combine proofs into a final proof. The paper reports that Aerie’s verification takes approximately 54 milliseconds on one CPU core, compared with about 6 milliseconds for leanVM in the authors’ comparison. Proving a batch of 32,768 signatures required approximately 2.1 GiB of peak memory. The short public salts account for most of the aggregate’s size. According to the paper, using one shared salt could reduce the aggregate from approximately 1.3 MiB to 66 KiB, but that approach relies on an additional security assumption the authors have not proved. These constraints mean that proving speed alone does not establish whether Aerie is suitable for replacing existing aggregation systems in blockchain consensus. Ethereum’s long-term roadmap includes replacing cryptographic components that could become vulnerable to future quantum computers. One approach under development uses hash-based signatures and leanVM, a zero-knowledge virtual machine designed to help aggregate those signatures efficiently. However, the a16z researchers argue that relying exclusively on hash-based cryptography could introduce additional computational costs and technical complexity. Thaler argued that lattice-based cryptography should remain under consideration as blockchains develop post-quantum systems. He said lattice-based proofs could reduce reliance on recursive proofs and custom hash-based signatures. He also argued that these design considerations should be weighed against the possibility of future attacks on established lattice assumptions. The researcher referred to the Ethereum Foundation ’s strawmap, which includes a hash-based layer-one approach and plans for native private transfers. He argued that public-key encryption for private transfers cannot be built from hash functions alone, so avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs would not eliminate every potential reliance on lattice cryptography. A separate proposal covered by The Crypto Times on October 14 explores how Bitcoin transactions could use post-quantum cryptography while limiting the amount of data stored on-chain . The proposal uses a mechanism called a degriefer to distinguish legitimate transactions from conflicting spends. Its stated goal is to reduce on-chain data storage, with a proposed transaction size of 96 bytes. Unlike the Bitcoin proposal, which focuses on the size of individual transactions, Aerie aggregates batches of signatures into a single proof. The authors said Aerie’s security relies on Falcon and Module-SIS, a lattice-based computational problem. They also reported that part of the system’s soundness proof was checked using the Lean 4 theorem prover. The paper discloses that AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic assisted with implementation, benchmarking, protocol development, and security proofs. The authors said they take responsibility for the paper’s accuracy. It also discloses that Thaler is an investor in blockchain-based platforms through a16z. Falcon is being standardized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology as FN-DSA. Changes to the final standard could affect aspects of Aerie’s design, including message hashing. The authors identify GPU acceleration, smaller aggregates through hidden salts, and proof merging as areas for further research. Further evaluation will be needed to assess Aerie’s suitability for distributed blockchain consensus. Most major blockchains besides Bitcoin run on proof of stake, where validators vote on each block by signing it. Signature aggregation is what makes large validator sets practical. Ethereum uses BLS signatures, whose algebraic structure lets it combine tens of thousands of validator signatures every slot into a single group element. Solana, where validator votes have made up about three-quarters of all transactions, is adopting BLS aggregation too, as part of its Alpenglow upgrade. But as useful as BLS is, it is not post-quantum — and in fact, no known post-quantum signature scheme aggregates this way. Post-quantum signatures are also 10 to 100 times larger than today’s elliptic-curve signatures, so without aggregation these signatures will bloat blocks — limiting throughput and raising the cost of running a node. This matters as blockchains carry a growing share of the world’s payments, from stablecoin transfers to payments made by AI agents. SNARKs (Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge) fix these issues: The “aggregate signature” becomes a single succinct proof that every signature in the batch verifies. The prevailing SNARK-based approach, central to Ethereum’s roadmap, pairs hash-based signatures with hash-based SNARKs. But this approach is slow because hash-based signatures are expensive to prove: A single laptop can’t keep up with a full slot of signatures, which is one reason Ethereum’s design splits the work across many provers and recursively merges their proofs. That’s why today we’re releasing Aerie , which takes the opposite approach by aggregating lattice-based signatures using lattice-based SNARKs . Aerie supports Falcon, a lattice-based signature scheme that NIST has selected for standardization, in both its Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 variants. Aerie is fast enough that a single laptop can aggregate roughly an Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures on its own: Aerie’s speed also makes a simpler aggregation design possible. In Ethereum’s current plan, each proof from leanVM (the zkVM being developed as part of Lean Ethereum to aggregate hash-based signatures) covers only about 900 signatures. Covering a full slot therefore takes rounds of recursive merging, and each round can’t start until the previous round’s proofs arrive. The first is Akita (the lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme we built with LayerZero Labs ), together with the sum-check-based proving techniques we developed on the road to Lattice Jolt. These techniques are highly parallel and well suited to GPUs , so Aerie has plenty of room to get even faster. The second reason Aerie is fast is the relative lack of hashing in lattice signature verification. Hash-based signatures are verified by evaluating hundreds of hashes per signature. Aggregating them means proving all of those hash evaluations — and hashing is expensive to prove, typically adding over 100x overhead relative to computing the hash natively. Lattice signatures are verified differently. The core checks are algebraic, and hashing plays only a small role: a handful of hash evaluations per signature, not hundreds. Falcon takes the lack of hashing especially far. It’s a hash-and-sign scheme whose hash takes only the message and a salt as input. So if the aggregate includes each signature’s salt, the verifier can compute every hash itself, and the proof needs to cover only the algebraic checks. That’s a big part of Aerie’s speed, and why we started with Falcon. Falcon is also compact: Falcon-1024 reaches NIST’s highest security level with signatures about half the size of ML-DSA-44’s, the lowest-security ML-DSA parameter set. We’re not suggesting every blockchain adopt Falcon. Its signing algorithm is complex, and it has historically been hard to fit on hardware wallets, relying on floating-point arithmetic and tens of kilobytes of working memory. Side-channel hardening is still an active area of work. But these drawbacks are being addressed rapidly. Recent research has shown how to implement Falcon signing with fixed-point arithmetic instead of floating point, and NIST now plans to require this approach in the FN-DSA standard. A new implementation also cuts Falcon-512 signing to about 11 kB of RAM, small enough for the secure elements in hardware wallets. For both reasons, Falcon is far easier to deploy than it was even a year ago. Hardware wallets are a challenge for stateless hash-based signatures too: The SPHINCS- variants light enough for a hardware wallet take from 47 seconds to over six minutes to sign on a Ledger secure element. For chains that weigh Falcon’s trade-offs and choose it — as Solana is exploring and Algorand has deployed — Aerie offers a fast path to aggregation. We’re also working on extensions that require proving some hashing: supporting ML-DSA, whose hash depends on the signature itself; and removing Falcon’s salts from the aggregate by proving its hash inside the SNARK. Recent advances like LaBinius offer paths to proving those few hashes efficiently. And we’re extending Aerie to hybrid signatures that pair a lattice signature with an elliptic-curve-based one, an important form of defense-in-depth. These extensions may not reach 50,000 signatures per second, but we still expect plenty of headroom over the 1,000 per second Ethereum has targeted . There’s an active debate about lattice versus hash-based cryptography in blockchain design, sharpened by speculation about what AI might mean for cryptanalysis . We’ll make the full case for embracing lattices in a future post. The short version is this: No one can promise that new attacks won’t be found on lattices, or on any other cryptography. But speculative cryptanalytic risk must be weighed against the clear and present risks built into more complicated systems. As noted above, Ethereum’s planned hash-only signature aggregation design relies on SNARK recursion, with the coordination overhead, bug surface, and unestablished security that come with that approach. Hash-only designs also lean on non-standard constructions: Ethereum’s planned consensus and account signatures are custom schemes outside NIST’s standards, with the underlying hash still undecided. This limits support from hardware wallets for individual users, and from the hardware security modules and custody systems that institutions rely on. Private payments need encryption, not just signatures and proofs: Recipients must learn about the notes sent to them, viewing keys must grant read access, and encrypted mempools must hide transactions until they’re ordered. Private payments matter to cypherpunks and financial institutions alike, and Ethereum already plans for them. The Ethereum Foundation’s strawmap , a draft long-term roadmap for its base layer, lists a private L1 with shielded transfers among its five “north stars,” alongside a hash-based post-quantum L1. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, and encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, yet encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide. A classic result of Russell Impagliazzo and Steven Rudich shows that public-key encryption cannot be built from hash functions in a black-box way. The best hash-only alternative, Merkle puzzles , gives honest users only a quadratic advantage over attackers, and this is optimal : No protocol can do better when hashes are modeled as random oracles. Even advocates of hash-only designs acknowledge this. So a private Ethereum, like any chain that supports private payments, will depend on structured cryptography somewhere in its stack — and in practice, that means lattices. ML-KEM, a lattice scheme, is NIST’s primary post-quantum encryption standard and is already deployed across much of the internet . Are there workarounds? One proposed solution is to keep encrypted notes off-chain, so fewer ciphertexts sit in public forever. But this doesn’t avoid encryption: The notes must still reach their recipients encrypted, over messaging apps and other channels that are already moving to ML-KEM. And off-chain delivery has trade-offs of its own: a channel that must stay available, can observe metadata, and whose failure can leave recipients unable to find and spend their funds. For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits. So the real question isn’t whether to rely on lattices, but whether to forgo their benefits for a false sense of security. An Aerie proof is about 66 KiB, whether it covers 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures or 16,384 Falcon-1024 signatures. That’s on par with the most compact prior lattice-based approach: PSE’s benchmarks of LaBRADOR-based Falcon aggregation report about 74 KB for 10,000 signatures, though verification there takes seconds rather than milliseconds. Because Aerie’s verifier computes each signature’s hash itself, it also needs each signature’s 40-byte salt. For large batches, the salts dominate: 32,768 of them take up about 1.3 MB, versus 66 KiB for the proof. Even so, the aggregate costs only about 42 bytes per signature, 16 times smaller than Falcon-512 signatures (666 bytes) and nearly 30 times smaller than Falcon-1024 signatures (1,280 bytes). Some deployments avoid the salt cost entirely. Algorand’s deterministic Falcon makes signing deterministic, which lets it replace the random per-signature salt with a fixed value. Aggregating its signatures would need no salts at all, just the 66 KiB proof, with small changes to how Aerie handles the salt and signature encoding. Measured against Falcon itself, Aerie’s prover is also cheap : On a single core, proving takes only about 8 times as long as standard Falcon verification of the same signatures, and 1.4 times as long as signing them. Compared with Orthus , the fastest prior Falcon aggregation scheme, Aerie (on one core of the same AVX-512 server): Moreover, Aerie proves everything a standard Falcon verifier checks. Prior Falcon aggregation work did not: It left out the check that each signature is canonically encoded, so its aggregates could accept signatures that a standard Falcon verifier would reject. We also compared Aerie with leanVM , which aggregates XMSS signatures, the stateful hash-based scheme Ethereum plans to use for consensus. On the same machine, Aerie aggregates 29x as many signatures per second (about 50,800 versus 1,770). Stateful signatures like XMSS work well at the consensus layer, where each validator signs at most one message per slot, so the slot number itself can serve as the signing state. But they pose large risks at the execution layer: A user who signs from two devices, or restores a wallet from a backup, can reuse signing state and thereby let attackers forge signatures under their key. That’s why Ethereum plans a stateless hash-based scheme for account signatures. And stateless hash-based signatures are even costlier to aggregate: In leanVM’s latest published benchmarks , on the same laptop model, it aggregates them at about 820 per second, roughly 60x slower than Aerie. (The benchmarked configuration also caps each key at about 127,000 signatures; configurations that allow far more cost more at key generation but aggregate just as fast.)

sources.title: Manufacturing Intelligence Report: The intelligent factory needs more than artificial intelligence - Manufacturing Today
passages: This is the central argument of The intelligent factory has an architecture problem , a new Manufacturing Intelligence Report 2026 from The Manufacturing Tech Brief.

Drawing on interviews with manufacturing and technology leaders, the report examines how industrial AI is changing the requirements for infrastructure, data integration, operational software and cybersecurity.

This approach is illustrated by a global electronics manufacturer operating more than 150 factories, where a real-time event architecture connected manufacturing information with supply chain planning, allowing changes that previously took days to gather, evaluate and distribute to be reflected in production plans in under an hour.
The improvement came not from replacing existing systems but from enabling information and decisions to move more effectively between them.

The next stage of intelligent manufacturing is unlikely to involve a universal technology platform or a single model for autonomous factories, because different production environments will continue to require different levels of automation, computing capability and human oversight.

The manufacturers making the greatest progress may therefore be those that connect intelligence to the operational context it needs, embed it into established workflows and ensure decisions remain trustworthy as technology becomes an integral part of production.
Jeremy Foster, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Cisco Compute, illustrates the changing importance of infrastructure.
“The network is to a modern AI factory what power distribution was to a manufacturing facility 50 years ago,” he says.
Dayan Rodriguez, Corporate Vice President of Manufacturing & Mobility at Microsoft, captures the broader change in the report.

Manufacturers have spent years connecting machines, integrating enterprise systems and collecting production data, creating an environment in which artificial intelligence can begin to influence how factories operate.
The challenge extends into cybersecurity, particularly as intelligent applications become more closely integrated with production equipment.

Many industrial assets cannot be patched, restarted or subjected to conventional security testing without disrupting operations, making it essential to design architectures that can contain threats and maintain production when individual systems fail.

Manufacturers must also establish clear boundaries around the authority given to AI, ensuring that increasingly sophisticated systems can support operational decisions without introducing unacceptable risks to safety, reliability or performance.
The challenge is no longer simply whether AI can detect equipment failures, optimize production schedules or identify quality problems.
Those capabilities are becoming increasingly accessible.

What remains harder is ensuring intelligent systems understand the operational environment, can access the information required to make reliable decisions and deliver results without introducing additional complexity.
The findings challenge a longstanding assumption that increasing connectivity and deploying more sophisticated applications will inevitably create smarter factories.
While these investments have improved operational visibility, they have not necessarily provided the foundations for intelligence to work effectively across different systems and facilities.

Rather than consolidating everything into one application, manufacturers need to preserve context as information moves between specialist systems , allowing equipment condition to be understood alongside production schedules, product information and wider business requirements.
The implications are significant for manufacturers trying to establish consistent digital strategies across multiple plants.
Different facilities may operate equipment installed decades apart, use different generations of industrial software and have varying levels of connectivity.
Introducing AI requires an approach that accommodates those differences without allowing every implementation to become a separate engineering project.
Consider a predictive maintenance system identifying deterioration in a critical machine.
The technical diagnosis may be accurate, but deciding what to do requires considerably more information.
Is alternative production capacity available?
How would an intervention affect delivery commitments?

extraction.body: Manufacturers have spent years connecting machines, integrating enterprise systems and collecting production data, creating an environment in which artificial intelligence can begin to influence how factories operate. Yet as AI moves beyond experimentation and becomes embedded in production, an increasingly important question is being overlooked. Are factories designed to support intelligence at scale? The challenge is no longer simply whether AI can detect equipment failures, optimize production schedules or identify quality problems. Those capabilities are becoming increasingly accessible. What remains harder is ensuring intelligent systems understand the operational environment, can access the information required to make reliable decisions and deliver results without introducing additional complexity. This is the central argument of The intelligent factory has an architecture problem , a new Manufacturing Intelligence Report 2026 from The Manufacturing Tech Brief. Drawing on interviews with manufacturing and technology leaders, the report examines how industrial AI is changing the requirements for infrastructure, data integration, operational software and cybersecurity. The findings challenge a longstanding assumption that increasing connectivity and deploying more sophisticated applications will inevitably create smarter factories. While these investments have improved operational visibility, they have not necessarily provided the foundations for intelligence to work effectively across different systems and facilities. A factory may have predictive maintenance software, advanced production analytics and AI-enabled quality inspection, but if those capabilities operate independently, the result may be another generation of technological silos. As AI begins influencing production rather than simply analyzing it, previously supporting technologies are becoming central to manufacturing performance. Industrial networks, computing infrastructure and data platforms increasingly determine how quickly information can be processed, where decisions can be made and whether intelligent applications operate reliably. The implications are significant for manufacturers trying to establish consistent digital strategies across multiple plants. Different facilities may operate equipment installed decades apart, use different generations of industrial software and have varying levels of connectivity. Introducing AI requires an approach that accommodates those differences without allowing every implementation to become a separate engineering project. Jeremy Foster, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Cisco Compute, illustrates the changing importance of infrastructure. “The network is to a modern AI factory what power distribution was to a manufacturing facility 50 years ago,” he says. As AI applications become more dependent on real-time information and increasingly influence physical processes, industrial connectivity is evolving from a supporting technology into a critical factor determining production performance, with network reliability and resilience shaping what manufacturing systems can achieve. Computing architecture is also evolving to accommodate different operational requirements, with workloads such as model training and enterprise analytics demanding substantial centralized resources, while applications including machine vision and real-time quality inspection require processing capabilities closer to the production equipment generating the data. Decisions about where intelligence operates therefore need to be driven by operational requirements rather than a general preference for cloud, edge or on-premises infrastructure. Manufacturers must also distinguish between collecting information and making it useful. Industrial equipment generates enormous quantities of data, but transmitting everything to a central platform increases costs without necessarily improving decisions. A more effective architecture processes information where it is relevant while ensuring important findings reach the people and systems capable of acting on them. One of the report’s most important arguments concerns the difference between operational visibility and operational understanding, as manufacturers increasingly rely on manufacturing execution systems (MES), enterprise resource planning (ERP), product lifecycle management (PLM), digital twins and specialist engineering applications that may provide accurate information within their own domains while remaining largely unaware of the consequences of events elsewhere. Consider a predictive maintenance system identifying deterioration in a critical machine. The technical diagnosis may be accurate, but deciding what to do requires considerably more information. What is the equipment producing? Which customer orders depend on it? Is alternative production capacity available? How would an intervention affect delivery commitments? Rather than consolidating everything into one application, manufacturers need to preserve context as information moves between specialist systems , allowing equipment condition to be understood alongside production schedules, product information and wider business requirements. This is changing the role of technologies such as MES, which can connect equipment data with production orders, materials and process conditions, while digital twins are evolving beyond visual representations into environments that support operational decisions. The objective is to ensure that information retains its meaning as it moves between systems, enabling manufacturers to understand not only what is happening in production but also the consequences for the wider business. Product information presents comparable challenges. An engineering change can affect procurement, inventory, production and potentially products already operating at customer sites. Understanding those consequences requires information to remain connected across the lifecycle without assuming every department uses the same software. The report presents the intelligent factory less as a collection of connected applications and more as an environment capable of coordinating decisions across specialist systems. This approach is illustrated by a global electronics manufacturer operating more than 150 factories, where a real-time event architecture connected manufacturing information with supply chain planning, allowing changes that previously took days to gather, evaluate and distribute to be reflected in production plans in under an hour. The improvement came not from replacing existing systems but from enabling information and decisions to move more effectively between them. As manufacturers give AI greater responsibility within operational workflows, the consequences of inaccurate information and poorly controlled systems become more serious. A dashboard containing an incorrect inventory figure may prompt an employee to investigate, but an automated system using the same information could initiate an inappropriate replenishment decision before anyone recognizes the problem. Data quality and governance therefore become essential to ensuring that intelligent systems understand what information means, where it originated and whether it is reliable enough to support a particular decision. The challenge extends into cybersecurity, particularly as intelligent applications become more closely integrated with production equipment. Many industrial assets cannot be patched, restarted or subjected to conventional security testing without disrupting operations, making it essential to design architectures that can contain threats and maintain production when individual systems fail. Manufacturers must also establish clear boundaries around the authority given to AI, ensuring that increasingly sophisticated systems can support operational decisions without introducing unacceptable risks to safety, reliability or performance. However, greater intelligence does not necessarily mean fully autonomous manufacturing, and some of the most credible applications involve AI supporting established engineering workflows rather than replacing experienced employees. In computer-aided manufacturing, for example, AI can assist with individual programming tasks while engineers review the results, while simulation allows teams to evaluate proposed operational changes before introducing them into live production. This approach recognizes that manufacturing decisions often carry physical consequences and that faster analysis does not eliminate the need for verification and accountability. Dayan Rodriguez, Corporate Vice President of Manufacturing & Mobility at Microsoft, captures the broader change in the report. “The manufacturers building sustainable AI strategies have stopped thinking about AI as a tool and started thinking about it as part of how their business operates,” he says. Integrating AI into established workflows also creates opportunities to preserve and extend valuable manufacturing knowledge. Experienced engineers understand equipment behavior, process limitations and unusual operating conditions that may not be adequately represented in formal documentation, and intelligent systems can help make that expertise available across a wider workforce. Rather than removing the need for skilled employees, the opportunity lies in supporting their decisions, accelerating learning and improving consistency across different facilities. The next stage of intelligent manufacturing is unlikely to involve a universal technology platform or a single model for autonomous factories, because different production environments will continue to require different levels of automation, computing capability and human oversight. The manufacturers making the greatest progress may therefore be those that connect intelligence to the operational context it needs, embed it into established workflows and ensure decisions remain trustworthy as technology becomes an integral part of production. The intelligent factory has an architecture problem Discover how manufacturing and technology leaders are rethinking industrial AI, edge computing, connected operations, data governance and cybersecurity. Drawing on industry interviews and practical examples, this 36-page report examines the architectural decisions shaping the next generation of intelligent factories. Free, expert-led sessions on AI, smart factories, and risk management. No travel. No cost. Just value.

This approach recognizes that manufacturing decisions often carry physical consequences and that faster analysis does not eliminate the need for verification and accountability.

Integrating AI into established workflows also creates opportunities to preserve and extend valuable manufacturing knowledge. Experienced engineers understand equipment behavior, process limitations and unusual operating conditions that may not be adequately represented in formal documentation, and intelligent systems can help make that expertise available across a wider workforce. Rather than removing the need for skilled employees, the opportunity lies in supporting their decisions, accelerating learning and improving consistency across different facilities.

The next stage of intelligent manufacturing is unlikely to involve a universal technology platform or a single model for autonomous factories, because different production environments will continue to require different levels of automation, computing capability and human oversight. The manufacturers making the greatest progress may therefore be those that connect intelligence to the operational context it needs, embed it into established workflows and ensure decisions remain trustworthy as technology becomes an integral part of production.

extraction.body: Express Computer - Digital Magazine, Latest Computer Magazine, India Manufacturing has entered a new era of competition — one where the decisive advantage no longer lies on the shop floor alone, but in the speed and quality of decisions made across the entire enterprise. For decades, industrial companies competed on scale, cost, and production capacity. Those advantages remain necessary, but they are no longer sufficient. Today, a raw material disruption, a cyber incident, or a sudden demand shift can ripple through operations in hours. The organisations that weather these pressures best are not simply the largest or most efficient — they are the most connected, the most informed, and the most adaptive. The technology agenda in manufacturing is being rewritten accordingly. Cloud modernization, IT-OT convergence, AI-driven operational intelligence, and cyber resilience have moved from the periphery of the CIO’s agenda to its very center — not as infrastructure projects, but as the foundations of competitive strategy. In this interview, Navin Nathani, a thought leader and a CIO at a leading manufacturing organisation shares how digital transformation is reshaping operations from the inside out: from ERP modernization that rebuilt trust across business teams, to AI applications that are quietly shifting manufacturing from reactive to predictive. The message is clear — technology is no longer a department within the business. It has become the operating system of the business itself. Our roadmap has therefore focused heavily on building connected operations where we are bringing plants, supply chain, finance and business teams onto a more integrated digital backbone. Cloud modernisation, SAP transformation, cybersecurity & AI led manufacturing intelligence became priorities because the business needed resilience and agility, not just better infrastructure. One thing I have learned in manufacturing is this, Technology projects succeed only when plant teams and business teams actually feel the need and want to see improvement in their daily work. One of the most impactful initiatives has been our SAP modernization and cloud transformation journey. For manufacturing companies, ERP is not just a system, it is operational reality. Procurement, production, finance, inventory and dispatch all depend on it. The migration helped us improve scalability, resilience and disaster recovery readiness significantly, but the bigger impact was operational confidence. Business teams today are far more comfortable embracing digital initiatives because they have seen stability improve firsthand. Another major area has been cybersecurity strengthening across the organization. Manufacturing companies today are increasingly vulnerable because plants are becoming more connected. Earlier, operational systems were isolated. Today, IT and OT environments are far more integrated, which creates both opportunity and risk. We have therefore invested heavily in proactive monitoring, governance and resilience focused controls. The biggest takeaway for me is this: Digital transformation becomes meaningful only when it quietly improves everyday business operations without employees constantly thinking about the technology behind it. What are the most promising AI-led use cases you are seeing within manufacturing operations today? The most practical AI use cases are the ones solving operational problems, not the ones creating excitement in presentations. Predictive maintenance is one area where AI is becoming genuinely valuable. In manufacturing, even a few hours of unexpected downtime can have a cascading business impact leading to millions of dollars in losses. AI-led insights are helping teams identify patterns earlier and respond proactively thus extending the life of these critical assets thereby reducing the capex needs. Another strong use case is intelligent supply & Demand planning with operational visibility. Manufacturing businesses generate enormous amounts of data every day, but historically a lot of it remained underutilised. AI is helping convert that data into usable decision support. One interesting shift is that employees are now more open to AI than before because they are beginning to see it as an assistant rather than a replacement. But AI only works well when the underlying processes are disciplined. If the operational data is inconsistent, AI simply amplifies the confusion faster. Therefore, clean core and clean data is a strategic imperative in manufacturing. Could you share a technology deployment that delivered stronger-than-expected outcomes? One thing I have consistently observed is that successful technology deployments create momentum beyond the project itself. Once business teams see one initiative working well, they become more willing to experiment and innovate further. Cybersecurity is becoming increasingly critical for manufacturing firms. How is your organization strengthening resilience across both IT and OT environments? Manufacturing cybersecurity has changed dramatically over the last few years. At the same time, we are working heavily on awareness because cybersecurity failures are rarely only technology failures. In manufacturing, a cyber incident can impact production schedules, customer deliveries and operational continuity very quickly. That makes cyber resilience a business priority, not just an IT responsibility. How important is IT-OT convergence within your organization’s long-term digital strategy? IT-OT convergence is becoming essential for modern manufacturing. Earlier, plant operations and enterprise technology largely operated independently. But real time manufacturing decisions today on critical KPI’s such as Yield, vibration, temperature, etc. rely on Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensors and edge-computing require both worlds to work together continuously. Without convergence, it becomes very difficult to achieve predictive operations, connected visibility or intelligent automation, all using secured communication layer. The organizations that will succeed are the ones that can bridge both perspectives instead of treating them as separate ecosystems. Looking ahead, what does the next phase of digital manufacturing transformation look like for your organisation? The next phase of manufacturing transformation will be far more intelligence led what is now called as Industrial AI. Earlier, digitization focused on capturing transactions and automating workflows. The next phase is about creating faster and better operational decisions using connected data. We are moving towards: AI-assisted plant operations Predictive supply chains Connected manufacturing ecosystems Cyber resilience by design Industrial IoT expansion Energy and sustainability intelligence Digital copilots for operational teams What excites me most is that manufacturing is finally becoming more proactive than reactive. Manufacturing has entered a new era of competition — one where the decisive advantage no longer lies on the shop floor alone, but in the speed and quality of decisions made across the entire enterprise.

For decades, industrial companies competed on scale, cost, and production capacity. Those advantages remain necessary, but they are no longer sufficient. Today, a raw material disruption, a cyber incident, or a sudden demand shift can ripple through operations in hours. The organisations that weather these pressures best are not simply the largest or most efficient — they are the most connected, the most informed, and the most adaptive.

The technology agenda in manufacturing is being rewritten accordingly. Cloud modernization, IT-OT convergence, AI-driven operational intelligence, and cyber resilience have moved from the periphery of the CIO’s agenda to its very center — not as infrastructure projects, but as the foundations of competitive strategy.

In this interview, Navin Nathani, a thought leader and a CIO at a leading manufacturing organisation shares how digital transformation is reshaping operations from the inside out: from ERP modernization that rebuilt trust across business teams, to AI applications that are quietly shifting manufacturing from reactive to predictive. The message is clear — technology is no longer a department within the business. It has become the operating system of the business itself.
Our roadmap has therefore focused heavily on building connected operations where we are bringing plants, supply chain, finance and business teams onto a more integrated digital backbone.
Cloud modernisation, SAP transformation, cybersecurity & AI led manufacturing intelligence became priorities because the business needed resilience and agility, not just better infrastructure.
One thing I have learned in manufacturing is this, Technology projects succeed only when plant teams and business teams actually feel the need and want to see improvement in their daily work.

One of the most impactful initiatives has been our SAP modernization and cloud transformation journey. For manufacturing companies, ERP is not just a system, it is operational reality. Procurement, production, finance, inventory and dispatch all depend on it.

The migration helped us improve scalability, resilience and disaster recovery readiness significantly, but the bigger impact was operational confidence. Business teams today are far more comfortable embracing digital initiatives because they have seen stability improve firsthand.
Another major area has been cybersecurity strengthening across the organization.

Manufacturing companies today are increasingly vulnerable because plants are becoming more connected. Earlier, operational systems were isolated. Today, IT and OT environments are far more integrated, which creates both opportunity and risk.

We have therefore invested heavily in proactive monitoring, governance and resilience focused controls. The biggest takeaway for me is this: Digital transformation becomes meaningful only when it quietly improves everyday business operations without employees constantly thinking about the technology behind it.
What are the most promising AI-led use cases you are seeing within manufacturing operations today?
The most practical AI use cases are the ones solving operational problems, not the ones creating excitement in presentations.

Predictive maintenance is one area where AI is becoming genuinely valuable. In manufacturing, even a few hours of unexpected downtime can have a cascading business impact leading to millions of dollars in losses. AI-led insights are helping teams identify patterns earlier and respond proactively thus extending the life of these critical assets thereby reducing the capex needs.

Another strong use case is intelligent supply & Demand planning with operational visibility. Manufacturing businesses generate enormous amounts of data every day, but historically a lot of it remained underutilised. AI is helping convert that data into usable decision support.
One interesting shift is that employees are now more open to AI than before because they are beginning to see it as an assistant rather than a replacement.

But AI only works well when the underlying processes are disciplined. If the operational data is inconsistent, AI simply amplifies the confusion faster. Therefore, clean core and clean data is a strategic imperative in manufacturing.
Could you share a technology deployment that delivered stronger-than-expected outcomes?

One thing I have consistently observed is that successful technology deployments create momentum beyond the project itself. Once business teams see one initiative working well, they become more willing to experiment and innovate further.
Cybersecurity is becoming increasingly critical for manufacturing firms. How is your organization strengthening resilience across both IT and OT environments?
Manufacturing cybersecurity has changed dramatically over the last few years.
At the same time, we are working heavily on awareness because cybersecurity failures are rarely only technology failures.

In manufacturing, a cyber incident can impact production schedules, customer deliveries and operational continuity very quickly. That makes cyber resilience a business priority, not just an IT responsibility.
How important is IT-OT convergence within your organization’s long-term digital strategy?
IT-OT convergence is becoming essential for modern manufacturing.

Earlier, plant operations and enterprise technology largely operated independently. But real time manufacturing decisions today on critical KPI’s such as Yield, vibration, temperature, etc. rely on Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensors and edge-computing require both worlds to work together continuously.
Without convergence, it becomes very difficult to achieve predictive operations, connected visibility or intelligent automation, all using secured communication layer.
The organizations that will succeed are the ones that can bridge both perspectives instead of treating them as separate ecosystems.

Earlier, digitization focused on capturing transactions and automating workflows. The next phase is about creating faster and better operational decisions using connected data.

sources.title: Manufacturing Intelligence Report: The intelligent factory needs more than artificial intelligence - Manufacturing Today
passages: This is the central argument of The intelligent factory has an architecture problem , a new Manufacturing Intelligence Report 2026 from The Manufacturing Tech Brief.

Drawing on interviews with manufacturing and technology leaders, the report examines how industrial AI is changing the requirements for infrastructure, data integration, operational software and cybersecurity.

This approach is illustrated by a global electronics manufacturer operating more than 150 factories, where a real-time event architecture connected manufacturing information with supply chain planning, allowing changes that previously took days to gather, evaluate and distribute to be reflected in production plans in under an hour.
The improvement came not from replacing existing systems but from enabling information and decisions to move more effectively between them.

The next stage of intelligent manufacturing is unlikely to involve a universal technology platform or a single model for autonomous factories, because different production environments will continue to require different levels of automation, computing capability and human oversight.

The manufacturers making the greatest progress may therefore be those that connect intelligence to the operational context it needs, embed it into established workflows and ensure decisions remain trustworthy as technology becomes an integral part of production.
Jeremy Foster, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Cisco Compute, illustrates the changing importance of infrastructure.
“The network is to a modern AI factory what power distribution was to a manufacturing facility 50 years ago,” he says.
Dayan Rodriguez, Corporate Vice President of Manufacturing & Mobility at Microsoft, captures the broader change in the report.

Manufacturers have spent years connecting machines, integrating enterprise systems and collecting production data, creating an environment in which artificial intelligence can begin to influence how factories operate.
The challenge extends into cybersecurity, particularly as intelligent applications become more closely integrated with production equipment.

Many industrial assets cannot be patched, restarted or subjected to conventional security testing without disrupting operations, making it essential to design architectures that can contain threats and maintain production when individual systems fail.

Manufacturers must also establish clear boundaries around the authority given to AI, ensuring that increasingly sophisticated systems can support operational decisions without introducing unacceptable risks to safety, reliability or performance.
The challenge is no longer simply whether AI can detect equipment failures, optimize production schedules or identify quality problems.
Those capabilities are becoming increasingly accessible.

What remains harder is ensuring intelligent systems understand the operational environment, can access the information required to make reliable decisions and deliver results without introducing additional complexity.
The findings challenge a longstanding assumption that increasing connectivity and deploying more sophisticated applications will inevitably create smarter factories.
While these investments have improved operational visibility, they have not necessarily provided the foundations for intelligence to work effectively across different systems and facilities.

Rather than consolidating everything into one application, manufacturers need to preserve context as information moves between specialist systems , allowing equipment condition to be understood alongside production schedules, product information and wider business requirements.
The implications are significant for manufacturers trying to establish consistent digital strategies across multiple plants.
Different facilities may operate equipment installed decades apart, use different generations of industrial software and have varying levels of connectivity.
Introducing AI requires an approach that accommodates those differences without allowing every implementation to become a separate engineering project.
Consider a predictive maintenance system identifying deterioration in a critical machine.
The technical diagnosis may be accurate, but deciding what to do requires considerably more information.
Is alternative production capacity available?
How would an intervention affect delivery commitments?
