extraction.body: Manufacturers have spent years connecting machines, integrating enterprise systems and collecting production data, creating an environment in which artificial intelligence can begin to influence how factories operate. Yet as AI moves beyond experimentation and becomes embedded in production, an increasingly important question is being overlooked. Are factories designed to support intelligence at scale? The challenge is no longer simply whether AI can detect equipment failures, optimize production schedules or identify quality problems. Those capabilities are becoming increasingly accessible. What remains harder is ensuring intelligent systems understand the operational environment, can access the information required to make reliable decisions and deliver results without introducing additional complexity. This is the central argument of The intelligent factory has an architecture problem , a new Manufacturing Intelligence Report 2026 from The Manufacturing Tech Brief. Drawing on interviews with manufacturing and technology leaders, the report examines how industrial AI is changing the requirements for infrastructure, data integration, operational software and cybersecurity. The findings challenge a longstanding assumption that increasing connectivity and deploying more sophisticated applications will inevitably create smarter factories. While these investments have improved operational visibility, they have not necessarily provided the foundations for intelligence to work effectively across different systems and facilities. A factory may have predictive maintenance software, advanced production analytics and AI-enabled quality inspection, but if those capabilities operate independently, the result may be another generation of technological silos. As AI begins influencing production rather than simply analyzing it, previously supporting technologies are becoming central to manufacturing performance. Industrial networks, computing infrastructure and data platforms increasingly determine how quickly information can be processed, where decisions can be made and whether intelligent applications operate reliably. The implications are significant for manufacturers trying to establish consistent digital strategies across multiple plants. Different facilities may operate equipment installed decades apart, use different generations of industrial software and have varying levels of connectivity. Introducing AI requires an approach that accommodates those differences without allowing every implementation to become a separate engineering project. Jeremy Foster, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Cisco Compute, illustrates the changing importance of infrastructure. “The network is to a modern AI factory what power distribution was to a manufacturing facility 50 years ago,” he says. As AI applications become more dependent on real-time information and increasingly influence physical processes, industrial connectivity is evolving from a supporting technology into a critical factor determining production performance, with network reliability and resilience shaping what manufacturing systems can achieve. Computing architecture is also evolving to accommodate different operational requirements, with workloads such as model training and enterprise analytics demanding substantial centralized resources, while applications including machine vision and real-time quality inspection require processing capabilities closer to the production equipment generating the data. Decisions about where intelligence operates therefore need to be driven by operational requirements rather than a general preference for cloud, edge or on-premises infrastructure. Manufacturers must also distinguish between collecting information and making it useful. Industrial equipment generates enormous quantities of data, but transmitting everything to a central platform increases costs without necessarily improving decisions. A more effective architecture processes information where it is relevant while ensuring important findings reach the people and systems capable of acting on them. One of the report’s most important arguments concerns the difference between operational visibility and operational understanding, as manufacturers increasingly rely on manufacturing execution systems (MES), enterprise resource planning (ERP), product lifecycle management (PLM), digital twins and specialist engineering applications that may provide accurate information within their own domains while remaining largely unaware of the consequences of events elsewhere. Consider a predictive maintenance system identifying deterioration in a critical machine. The technical diagnosis may be accurate, but deciding what to do requires considerably more information. What is the equipment producing? Which customer orders depend on it? Is alternative production capacity available? How would an intervention affect delivery commitments? Rather than consolidating everything into one application, manufacturers need to preserve context as information moves between specialist systems , allowing equipment condition to be understood alongside production schedules, product information and wider business requirements. This is changing the role of technologies such as MES, which can connect equipment data with production orders, materials and process conditions, while digital twins are evolving beyond visual representations into environments that support operational decisions. The objective is to ensure that information retains its meaning as it moves between systems, enabling manufacturers to understand not only what is happening in production but also the consequences for the wider business. Product information presents comparable challenges. An engineering change can affect procurement, inventory, production and potentially products already operating at customer sites. Understanding those consequences requires information to remain connected across the lifecycle without assuming every department uses the same software. The report presents the intelligent factory less as a collection of connected applications and more as an environment capable of coordinating decisions across specialist systems. This approach is illustrated by a global electronics manufacturer operating more than 150 factories, where a real-time event architecture connected manufacturing information with supply chain planning, allowing changes that previously took days to gather, evaluate and distribute to be reflected in production plans in under an hour. The improvement came not from replacing existing systems but from enabling information and decisions to move more effectively between them. As manufacturers give AI greater responsibility within operational workflows, the consequences of inaccurate information and poorly controlled systems become more serious. A dashboard containing an incorrect inventory figure may prompt an employee to investigate, but an automated system using the same information could initiate an inappropriate replenishment decision before anyone recognizes the problem. Data quality and governance therefore become essential to ensuring that intelligent systems understand what information means, where it originated and whether it is reliable enough to support a particular decision. The challenge extends into cybersecurity, particularly as intelligent applications become more closely integrated with production equipment. Many industrial assets cannot be patched, restarted or subjected to conventional security testing without disrupting operations, making it essential to design architectures that can contain threats and maintain production when individual systems fail. Manufacturers must also establish clear boundaries around the authority given to AI, ensuring that increasingly sophisticated systems can support operational decisions without introducing unacceptable risks to safety, reliability or performance. However, greater intelligence does not necessarily mean fully autonomous manufacturing, and some of the most credible applications involve AI supporting established engineering workflows rather than replacing experienced employees. In computer-aided manufacturing, for example, AI can assist with individual programming tasks while engineers review the results, while simulation allows teams to evaluate proposed operational changes before introducing them into live production. This approach recognizes that manufacturing decisions often carry physical consequences and that faster analysis does not eliminate the need for verification and accountability. Dayan Rodriguez, Corporate Vice President of Manufacturing & Mobility at Microsoft, captures the broader change in the report. “The manufacturers building sustainable AI strategies have stopped thinking about AI as a tool and started thinking about it as part of how their business operates,” he says. Integrating AI into established workflows also creates opportunities to preserve and extend valuable manufacturing knowledge. Experienced engineers understand equipment behavior, process limitations and unusual operating conditions that may not be adequately represented in formal documentation, and intelligent systems can help make that expertise available across a wider workforce. Rather than removing the need for skilled employees, the opportunity lies in supporting their decisions, accelerating learning and improving consistency across different facilities. The next stage of intelligent manufacturing is unlikely to involve a universal technology platform or a single model for autonomous factories, because different production environments will continue to require different levels of automation, computing capability and human oversight. The manufacturers making the greatest progress may therefore be those that connect intelligence to the operational context it needs, embed it into established workflows and ensure decisions remain trustworthy as technology becomes an integral part of production. The intelligent factory has an architecture problem Discover how manufacturing and technology leaders are rethinking industrial AI, edge computing, connected operations, data governance and cybersecurity. Drawing on industry interviews and practical examples, this 36-page report examines the architectural decisions shaping the next generation of intelligent factories. Free, expert-led sessions on AI, smart factories, and risk management. No travel. No cost. Just value.

extraction.body: Who gets Satoshi Nakamoto’s 1.1 million bitcoin, and, for that matter, millions more that are at risk if quantum computers become powerful enough to break the security protecting it, has been a topic of intense debate for quite some time. Christopher Smith, CEO of quantum-resistant layer-1 blockchain Quantus, believes whoever develops that technology first could take those tokens worth billions, potentially with government backing. “The most likely scenario is that whoever gets the first CRQC (Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer) will take them, probably with the blessing of whichever national government,” Smith told CoinDesk. “Hopefully it’s a government that likes bitcoin.” The security researcher and protocol engineer’s warning comes as nine crypto companies unveiled the Quantum Alliance on Thursday to develop common security standards for bitcoin, Ethereum and other blockchain networks. The concern is that future quantum computers could reverse-engineer a wallet’s publicly visible key to uncover its secret key, allowing attackers to steal funds. The Alliance estimates that 6.4 million bitcoin, or 30.2% of the supply, have public keys already exposed. Those coins, it clarified, cannot be stolen this way today because no existing quantum computer is yet powerful enough. The first question many are asking today is when quantum computers will actually be a threat to bitcoin. Bryn Bennett, chief revenue officer at The Vault, responded: “Nobody knows the date, but the estimates keep falling, and the risk is one we can already plan for. The question for custodians isn’t whether the date is 2028 or 2035; it’s whether you can migrate in time if it arrives early.” Richard Carback, chief technology officer of Postquant Labs, disagreed, saying he believes 2028 is a realistic date for a machine capable of breaking today’s cryptography. Recent research has reduced estimates of the computing power needed to attack bitcoin and Ethereum. But no existing machine can break their cryptography, and predictions about when one might arrive remain disputed. The prospect of those BTC tokens being stolen raises yet another difficult question: should developers freeze vulnerable assets, such as Bitcoin holdings, before quantum computers can reach them? Carback says he prefers that they be moved rather than frozen, while Bennet sees a different problem. “Nobody owns that issue, and that’s the problem,” Bennett told CoinDesk. “A custodian protects its clients’ assets, not abandoned ones. Freezing coins is a governance decision for the Bitcoin network, not for the industry.” “Any freeze would trade quantum risk for a precedent on property rights and neutrality,” he added. The debate has been ongoing. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao suggested freezing Satoshi’s estimated 1.1 million bitcoin if the coins remain untouched as quantum technology advances. Bitcoin developer Jameson Lopp has also proposed restrictions on vulnerable coins to prevent future theft. But critics argue that freezing someone’s bitcoin goes against the promise that no one can confiscate it. Making bitcoin quantum-resistant would mean replacing the digital signatures used to authorize transactions. That requires agreement among developers, miners, wallet providers, exchanges and users. “Nobody has a credible single number, and anyone offering one is guessing,” Bennett said of the cost. “The real cost isn’t the cryptography; it’s coordinating wallets, exchanges, custodians and protocol developers.” The replacement signatures could also take up more space on the blockchain, potentially increasing fees or reducing the number of transactions bitcoin can process. Researchers are already working on ways to limit that impact. The Quantum Alliance, whose members include Hacken, Charles Hoskinson’s Midnight Foundation, Quantus and Postquant Labs, plans to publish common security tests and guidance for moving existing networks to quantum-resistant systems. Carback also proposed placing vulnerable coins in a trust, allowing owners who can prove ownership to recover their funds. For bitcoin holders, the unresolved question is whether the network can protect their money without changing the rules that made the number one cryptocurrency so appealing in the first place. The debate has been ongoing. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao suggested freezing Satoshi’s estimated 1.1 million bitcoin if the coins remain untouched as quantum technology advances. Bitcoin developer Jameson Lopp has also proposed restrictions on vulnerable coins to prevent future theft. But critics argue that freezing someone’s bitcoin goes against the promise that no one can confiscate it.
Making bitcoin quantum-resistant would mean replacing the digital signatures used to authorize transactions. That requires agreement among developers, miners, wallet providers, exchanges and users.

“Nobody has a credible single number, and anyone offering one is guessing,” Bennett said of the cost. “The real cost isn’t the cryptography; it’s coordinating wallets, exchanges, custodians and protocol developers.”

The replacement signatures could also take up more space on the blockchain, potentially increasing fees or reducing the number of transactions bitcoin can process. Researchers are already working on ways to limit that impact.

The Quantum Alliance, whose members include Hacken, Charles Hoskinson’s Midnight Foundation, Quantus and Postquant Labs, plans to publish common security tests and guidance for moving existing networks to quantum-resistant systems.

Carback also proposed placing vulnerable coins in a trust, allowing owners who can prove ownership to recover their funds. For bitcoin holders, the unresolved question is whether the network can protect their money without changing the rules that made the number one cryptocurrency so appealing in the first place.

extraction.body: Who gets Satoshi Nakamoto’s 1.1 million bitcoin, and, for that matter, millions more that are at risk if quantum computers become powerful enough to break the security protecting it, has been a topic of intense debate for quite some time. Christopher Smith, CEO of quantum-resistant layer-1 blockchain Quantus, believes whoever develops that technology first could take those tokens worth billions, potentially with government backing. “The most likely scenario is that whoever gets the first CRQC (Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer) will take them, probably with the blessing of whichever national government,” Smith told CoinDesk. “Hopefully it’s a government that likes bitcoin.” The security researcher and protocol engineer’s warning comes as nine crypto companies unveiled the Quantum Alliance on Thursday to develop common security standards for bitcoin, Ethereum and other blockchain networks. The concern is that future quantum computers could reverse-engineer a wallet’s publicly visible key to uncover its secret key, allowing attackers to steal funds. The Alliance estimates that 6.4 million bitcoin, or 30.2% of the supply, have public keys already exposed. Those coins, it clarified, cannot be stolen this way today because no existing quantum computer is yet powerful enough. The first question many are asking today is when quantum computers will actually be a threat to bitcoin. Bryn Bennett, chief revenue officer at The Vault, responded: “Nobody knows the date, but the estimates keep falling, and the risk is one we can already plan for. The question for custodians isn’t whether the date is 2028 or 2035; it’s whether you can migrate in time if it arrives early.” Richard Carback, chief technology officer of Postquant Labs, disagreed, saying he believes 2028 is a realistic date for a machine capable of breaking today’s cryptography. Recent research has reduced estimates of the computing power needed to attack bitcoin and Ethereum. But no existing machine can break their cryptography, and predictions about when one might arrive remain disputed. The prospect of those BTC tokens being stolen raises yet another difficult question: should developers freeze vulnerable assets, such as Bitcoin holdings, before quantum computers can reach them? Carback says he prefers that they be moved rather than frozen, while Bennet sees a different problem. “Nobody owns that issue, and that’s the problem,” Bennett told CoinDesk. “A custodian protects its clients’ assets, not abandoned ones. Freezing coins is a governance decision for the Bitcoin network, not for the industry.” “Any freeze would trade quantum risk for a precedent on property rights and neutrality,” he added. The debate has been ongoing. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao suggested freezing Satoshi’s estimated 1.1 million bitcoin if the coins remain untouched as quantum technology advances. Bitcoin developer Jameson Lopp has also proposed restrictions on vulnerable coins to prevent future theft. But critics argue that freezing someone’s bitcoin goes against the promise that no one can confiscate it. Making bitcoin quantum-resistant would mean replacing the digital signatures used to authorize transactions. That requires agreement among developers, miners, wallet providers, exchanges and users. “Nobody has a credible single number, and anyone offering one is guessing,” Bennett said of the cost. “The real cost isn’t the cryptography; it’s coordinating wallets, exchanges, custodians and protocol developers.” The replacement signatures could also take up more space on the blockchain, potentially increasing fees or reducing the number of transactions bitcoin can process. Researchers are already working on ways to limit that impact. The Quantum Alliance, whose members include Hacken, Charles Hoskinson’s Midnight Foundation, Quantus and Postquant Labs, plans to publish common security tests and guidance for moving existing networks to quantum-resistant systems. Carback also proposed placing vulnerable coins in a trust, allowing owners who can prove ownership to recover their funds. For bitcoin holders, the unresolved question is whether the network can protect their money without changing the rules that made the number one cryptocurrency so appealing in the first place. extraction.body: By: Dan La Botz October 16, 2026 [PDF] [Print] Mikel, a housing activist in an encampmen in Bilbao, Spain. [Bilbao, Spain, October 15, 2026] Hundreds of thousands have marched in Spain in recent weeks to stop evictions, in opposition to housing speculation, against rising rent, and to demand more housing. One woman’s eviction sparked the movement. On September 23 María del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from the home where she had lived for 70 years. A lower court ordered her return to her home, but the Spanish Supreme Court overturned that ruling and she died in a hospital on October 7. Those events came to symbolize the housing struggle and brought the people of Spain into the streets. There have been massive marches and occupations of public spaces in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities, including here in Bilbao, the largest city in Euskadi (the Basque Country). Some local housing activists, about fifty of them, have set up an encampment, a tent city, in front of the massive, squat, neo-baroque Arriaga Theater in the heart of Bilbao. These housing activists who have been spending their nights in tents now for three weeks, though the encampment is about to end because, according to a young activist interviewed by VoxPopuli , they can no longer continue the fight in this way, “we’re tired, we’re burned out,” though he promises that they will participate in the protest march this weekend and in the general strike called for November 11 by the labor unions. I enter the encampment, ask if someone can speak with me, an American leftist journalist, and a young man named Mikel offers to talk, though he prefers not to use his last name. “We established this encampment three weeks ago as part of our fight for housing. We also join with the unions in the marches and rallies. We believe that housing is a basic right. People are entitled to decent housing.” In fact, Article 47 of the Spanish Constitution states that all Spaniards have a right to “decent and adequate housing,” though this is a “guiding principle” rather than a legal right that can be enforced. So, in 2023, Spain adopted a Housing Law intended to regulate rents, protect tenants, and curb speculation. This year, a new housing law intended to stop evictions of the vulnerable, protect tenants, and cap rents was adopted, then rejected, then re-approved a weaker measure. Mikel, however, feels that both Euskadi’s autonomous government, headed by centrist President Imanol Pradales, as well as the Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of the Socialist Party who has been in power for eight years, have failed the people. The housing crisis led President Sanchez to call snap elections which will take place on November 29, thinking the movement, including the general strike, could assure his victory. Now, however, it seems they could lead to his defeat and a victory for the rightwing People’s Party and the far-right Vox party but he would rather be fighting over housing than over immigration. “They talk about improving the housing situation, but they haven’t done it,” says Mikel, “They don’t intervene to control the housing market. There’s a disenchantment with the parties of the left.” In fact, over the past decade both the Spanish and Euskadi governments, have failed to resolve the housing crisis. According to the Bank of Spain there is a shortage of between 750,000 and more than a million homes. The global and Eurozone crises of 2008 and 2009 led to bankruptcies and evictions as what Mikel calls “vulture funds” moved in to take over housing being abandoned by former owners. Those financiers have continued to dominate the market. Speculating, but not building homes. In addition. social and public housing accounts for only about 2.5% to 3.3% of Spain’s total residential stock, compared to about 10% for the European Union and as much as 20% in Sweden. The Spanish far right parties blame the housing crisis entirely on immigration. In the last decade, Spain’s population grew from 46.42 million to 49.8 million, a growth of 3.38 million, all of it the result of immigration. But in that decade, Spain built only 800,000 to 850,000 new homes when hundreds of thousands more were needed. The increased demand for housing has led to the rising rents. And it is true that with the Socialist Party’s liberal immigration policies the immigrant population grew rapidly. Still, it is those immigrants who made it possible for Spain to maintain and expand its population, since the country has one of the lowest birthrates in the European Union, with a fertility rate below the generational replacement level. Those immigrants from Latin America and Morocco have also been an important factor in the success of Spain’s economy relative to the rest of Europe. The problem isn’t immigration, it’s wages, volunteer several activists in the encampment who are listening to Mikel and me as we talk. “I used to work in public transportation,” says one woman. “With those wages there is no way to keep up with rising rents.” Another woman says, “With my wages it would be impossible for me to ever pay off a mortgage.” And, according to economic studies, they’re right. Rents have been rising seven times faster than wages, and today working people in Spain use 50% of their wages to pay their rent, while not long ago they used only 30%. “We need rent freezes,” says Mikel. “We’re not asking for anything extravagant,” he says, “we just want decent housing.” Please donate to New Politics to allow us to continue bringing you independent, sharp, and provocative political analysis. [Bilbao, Spain, October 15, 2026] Hundreds of thousands have marched in Spain in recent weeks to stop evictions, in opposition to housing speculation, against rising rent, and to demand more housing. One woman’s eviction sparked the movement. On September 23 María del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from the home where she had lived for 70 years. A lower court ordered her return to her home, but the Spanish Supreme Court overturned that ruling and she died in a hospital on October 7. Those events came to symbolize the housing struggle and brought the people of Spain into the streets.

There have been massive marches and occupations of public spaces in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities, including here in Bilbao, the largest city in Euskadi (the Basque Country). Some local housing activists, about fifty of them, have set up an encampment, a tent city, in front of the massive, squat, neo-baroque Arriaga Theater in the heart of Bilbao.

These housing activists who have been spending their nights in tents now for three weeks, though the encampment is about to end because, according to a young activist interviewed by VoxPopuli , they can no longer continue the fight in this way, “we’re tired, we’re burned out,” though he promises that they will participate in the protest march this weekend and in the general strike called for November 11 by the labor unions.
I enter the encampment, ask if someone can speak with me, an American leftist journalist, and a young man named Mikel offers to talk, though he prefers not to use his last name.

“We established this encampment three weeks ago as part of our fight for housing. We also join with the unions in the marches and rallies. We believe that housing is a basic right. People are entitled to decent housing.”

In fact, Article 47 of the Spanish Constitution states that all Spaniards have a right to “decent and adequate housing,” though this is a “guiding principle” rather than a legal right that can be enforced. So, in 2023, Spain adopted a Housing Law intended to regulate rents, protect tenants, and curb speculation. This year, a new housing law intended to stop evictions of the vulnerable, protect tenants, and cap rents was adopted, then rejected, then re-approved a weaker measure.

Mikel, however, feels that both Euskadi’s autonomous government, headed by centrist President Imanol Pradales, as well as the Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of the Socialist Party who has been in power for eight years, have failed the people.

The housing crisis led President Sanchez to call snap elections which will take place on November 29, thinking the movement, including the general strike, could assure his victory. Now, however, it seems they could lead to his defeat and a victory for the rightwing People’s Party and the far-right Vox party but he would rather be fighting over housing than over immigration.
“They talk about improving the housing situation, but they haven’t done it,” says Mikel, “They don’t intervene to control the housing market. There’s a disenchantment with the parties of the left.”

In fact, over the past decade both the Spanish and Euskadi governments, have failed to resolve the housing crisis. According to the Bank of Spain there is a shortage of between 750,000 and more than a million homes. The global and Eurozone crises of 2008 and 2009 led to bankruptcies and evictions as what Mikel calls “vulture funds” moved in to take over housing being abandoned by former owners. Those financiers have continued to dominate the market. Speculating, but not building homes. In addition. social and public housing accounts for only about 2.5% to 3.3% of Spain’s total residential stock, compared to about 10% for the European Union and as much as 20% in Sweden.

The Spanish far right parties blame the housing crisis entirely on immigration. In the last decade, Spain’s population grew from 46.42 million to 49.8 million, a growth of 3.38 million, all of it the result of immigration. But in that decade, Spain built only 800,000 to 850,000 new homes when hundreds of thousands more were needed.

The increased demand for housing has led to the rising rents. And it is true that with the Socialist Party’s liberal immigration policies the immigrant population grew rapidly. Still, it is those immigrants who made it possible for Spain to maintain and expand its population, since the country has one of the lowest birthrates in the European Union, with a fertility rate below the generational replacement level. Those immigrants from Latin America and Morocco have also been an important factor in the success of Spain’s economy relative to the rest of Europe.
The problem isn’t immigration, it’s wages, volunteer several activists in the encampment who are listening to Mikel and me as we talk.
“I used to work in public transportation,” says one woman. “With those wages there is no way to keep up with rising rents.”
Another woman says, “With my wages it would be impossible for me to ever pay off a mortgage.”

And, according to economic studies, they’re right. Rents have been rising seven times faster than wages, and today working people in Spain use 50% of their wages to pay their rent, while not long ago they used only 30%.
“We need rent freezes,” says Mikel. “We’re not asking for anything extravagant,” he says, “we just want decent housing.”

extraction.body: By: Dan La Botz October 16, 2026 [PDF] [Print] Mikel, a housing activist in an encampmen in Bilbao, Spain. [Bilbao, Spain, October 15, 2026] Hundreds of thousands have marched in Spain in recent weeks to stop evictions, in opposition to housing speculation, against rising rent, and to demand more housing. One woman’s eviction sparked the movement. On September 23 María del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from the home where she had lived for 70 years. A lower court ordered her return to her home, but the Spanish Supreme Court overturned that ruling and she died in a hospital on October 7. Those events came to symbolize the housing struggle and brought the people of Spain into the streets. There have been massive marches and occupations of public spaces in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities, including here in Bilbao, the largest city in Euskadi (the Basque Country). Some local housing activists, about fifty of them, have set up an encampment, a tent city, in front of the massive, squat, neo-baroque Arriaga Theater in the heart of Bilbao. These housing activists who have been spending their nights in tents now for three weeks, though the encampment is about to end because, according to a young activist interviewed by VoxPopuli , they can no longer continue the fight in this way, “we’re tired, we’re burned out,” though he promises that they will participate in the protest march this weekend and in the general strike called for November 11 by the labor unions. I enter the encampment, ask if someone can speak with me, an American leftist journalist, and a young man named Mikel offers to talk, though he prefers not to use his last name. “We established this encampment three weeks ago as part of our fight for housing. We also join with the unions in the marches and rallies. We believe that housing is a basic right. People are entitled to decent housing.” In fact, Article 47 of the Spanish Constitution states that all Spaniards have a right to “decent and adequate housing,” though this is a “guiding principle” rather than a legal right that can be enforced. So, in 2023, Spain adopted a Housing Law intended to regulate rents, protect tenants, and curb speculation. This year, a new housing law intended to stop evictions of the vulnerable, protect tenants, and cap rents was adopted, then rejected, then re-approved a weaker measure. Mikel, however, feels that both Euskadi’s autonomous government, headed by centrist President Imanol Pradales, as well as the Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of the Socialist Party who has been in power for eight years, have failed the people. The housing crisis led President Sanchez to call snap elections which will take place on November 29, thinking the movement, including the general strike, could assure his victory. Now, however, it seems they could lead to his defeat and a victory for the rightwing People’s Party and the far-right Vox party but he would rather be fighting over housing than over immigration. “They talk about improving the housing situation, but they haven’t done it,” says Mikel, “They don’t intervene to control the housing market. There’s a disenchantment with the parties of the left.” In fact, over the past decade both the Spanish and Euskadi governments, have failed to resolve the housing crisis. According to the Bank of Spain there is a shortage of between 750,000 and more than a million homes. The global and Eurozone crises of 2008 and 2009 led to bankruptcies and evictions as what Mikel calls “vulture funds” moved in to take over housing being abandoned by former owners. Those financiers have continued to dominate the market. Speculating, but not building homes. In addition. social and public housing accounts for only about 2.5% to 3.3% of Spain’s total residential stock, compared to about 10% for the European Union and as much as 20% in Sweden. The Spanish far right parties blame the housing crisis entirely on immigration. In the last decade, Spain’s population grew from 46.42 million to 49.8 million, a growth of 3.38 million, all of it the result of immigration. But in that decade, Spain built only 800,000 to 850,000 new homes when hundreds of thousands more were needed. The increased demand for housing has led to the rising rents. And it is true that with the Socialist Party’s liberal immigration policies the immigrant population grew rapidly. Still, it is those immigrants who made it possible for Spain to maintain and expand its population, since the country has one of the lowest birthrates in the European Union, with a fertility rate below the generational replacement level. Those immigrants from Latin America and Morocco have also been an important factor in the success of Spain’s economy relative to the rest of Europe. The problem isn’t immigration, it’s wages, volunteer several activists in the encampment who are listening to Mikel and me as we talk. “I used to work in public transportation,” says one woman. “With those wages there is no way to keep up with rising rents.” Another woman says, “With my wages it would be impossible for me to ever pay off a mortgage.” And, according to economic studies, they’re right. Rents have been rising seven times faster than wages, and today working people in Spain use 50% of their wages to pay their rent, while not long ago they used only 30%. “We need rent freezes,” says Mikel. “We’re not asking for anything extravagant,” he says, “we just want decent housing.” Please donate to New Politics to allow us to continue bringing you independent, sharp, and provocative political analysis. [Bilbao, Spain, October 15, 2026] Hundreds of thousands have marched in Spain in recent weeks to stop evictions, in opposition to housing speculation, against rising rent, and to demand more housing. One woman’s eviction sparked the movement. [ 1 ]

On September 23 María del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from the home where she had lived for 70 years. A lower court ordered her return to her home, but the Spanish Supreme Court overturned that ruling and she died in a hospital on October 7. Those events came to symbolize the housing struggle and brought the people of Spain into the streets. There have been massive marches and occupations of public spaces in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities, including here in Bilbao , the largest city in Euskadi (the Basque Country). Some local housing activists, about fifty of them, have set up an encampment, a tent city, in front of the massive, squat, neo-baroque Arriaga Theater in the heart of Bilbao.

These housing activists who have been spending their nights in tents now for three weeks, though the encampment is about to end because, according to a young activist interviewed by VoxPopuli , they can no longer continue the fight in this way, “we’re tired, we’re burned out,” though he promises that they will participate in the protest march this weekend and in the general strike called for November 11 by the labor unions.
I enter the encampment, ask if someone can speak with me, an American leftist journalist, and a young man named Mikel offers to talk, though he prefers not to use his last name.

“We established this encampment three weeks ago as part of our fight for housing. We also join with the unions in the marches and rallies. We believe that housing is a basic right. People are entitled to decent housing.”

In fact, Article 47 of the Spanish Constitution states that all Spaniards have a right to “decent and adequate housing,” though this is a “guiding principle” rather than a legal right that can be enforced. So, in 2023, Spain adopted a Housing Law intended to regulate rents, protect tenants, and curb speculation. This year, a new housing law intended to stop evictions of the vulnerable, protect tenants, and cap rents was adopted, then rejected, then re-approved a weaker measure.

Mikel, however, feels that both Euskadi’s autonomous government, headed by centrist President Imanol Pradales, as well as the Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of the Socialist Party who has been in power for eight years, have failed the people.

The housing crisis led President Sanchez to call snap elections which will take place on November 29 , thinking the movement, including the general strike, could assure his victory. Now, however, it seems they could lead to his defeat and a victory for the rightwing People’s Party and the far-right Vox party but he would rather be fighting over housing than over immigration.
“They talk about improving the housing situation, but they haven’t done it,” says Mikel, “They don’t intervene to control the housing market. There’s a disenchantment with the parties of the left.”

In fact, over the past decade both the Spanish and Euskadi governments, have failed to resolve the housing crisis. According to the Bank of Spain there is a shortage of between 750,000 and more than a million homes. The global and Eurozone crises of 2008 and 2009 led to bankruptcies and evictions as what Mikel calls “vulture funds” moved in to take over housing being abandoned by former owners. Those financiers have continued to dominate the market. Speculating, but not building homes. In addition. social and public housing accounts for only about 2.5% to 3.3% of Spain’s total residential stock, compared to about 10% for the European Union and as much as 20% in Sweden.

The Spanish far right parties blame the housing crisis entirely on immigration. In the last decade, Spain’s population grew from 46.42 million to 49.8 million, a growth of 3.38 million, all of it the result of immigration. But in that decade, Spain built only 800,000 to 850,000 new homes when hundreds of thousands more were needed.

The increased demand for housing has led to the rising rents. And it is true that with the Socialist Party’s liberal immigration policies the immigrant population grew rapidly. Still, it is those immigrants who made it possible for Spain to maintain and expand its population, since the country has one of the lowest birthrates in the European Union, with a fertility rate below the generational replacement level. Those immigrants from Latin America and Morocco have also been an important factor in the success of Spain’s economy relative to the rest of Europe.
The problem isn’t immigration, it’s wages, volunteer several activists in the encampment who are listening to Mikel and me as we talk.
“I used to work in public transportation,” says one woman. “With those wages there is no way to keep up with rising rents.”
Another woman says, “With my wages it would be impossible for me to ever pay off a mortgage.”

And, according to economic studies, they’re right. Rents have been rising seven times faster than wages, and today working people in Spain use 50% of their wages to pay their rent, while not long ago they used only 30%.
“We need rent freezes,” says Mikel. “We’re not asking for anything extravagant,” he says, “we just want decent housing.”

The regulator will invite views on the proposed designation and will then make a final decision by February.

sources.title: Crypto Price Today: Bitcoin and Ethereum Recover Modestly After Inflation-Driven Dip - The Crypto Times
passages: In response, Bitcoin and Ethereum both sold off sharply, with the decline amplified by forced liquidations in leveraged derivatives markets.
CoinGlass data indicated total crypto liquidations approached or exceeded $900 million to nearly $1 billion over a 24-hour window on October 15, with the large majority occurring in long positions.
Ethereum and Bitcoin together accounted for a substantial share of those liquidations, as leveraged traders were stopped out near the session lows.
Such liquidation cascades are a recurring feature of crypto markets when prices move quickly against concentrated leveraged positions.
Once initial stops are triggered, forced selling can push prices lower, hitting additional stops and creating a feedback loop until new buyers absorb the supply.
In this instance, the process appeared to exhaust itself near the $79,800–80,000 area for Bitcoin and corresponding support for Ethereum, after which prices recovered.
Funding rates in perpetual futures have remained relatively contained post-event, suggesting that extreme one-sided leverage has been reduced for the moment.
The information presented is for informational purposes and does not constitute investment advice.
Ethereum’s 24-hour range of roughly $2,325 to $2,463 shows it successfully defended support near the lower end of the recent band.
Relative strength against Bitcoin has improved modestly over the past day, though the longer-term ETH/BTC ratio remains a focus for traders monitoring capital rotation between the two largest assets.
Looking ahead, market participants will monitor subsequent economic releases, Federal Reserve communications, and any shifts in institutional positioning.
Bitcoin’s ability to hold above the low $80,000s and Ethereum’s capacity to sustain levels above $2,400 will be watched as near-term technical references.

Both assets continue to trade with substantial discounts to their 2025 highs, leaving room for either further consolidation or renewed directional moves depending on incoming data and broader risk sentiment.
According to data from CoinGecko as of approximately 05:50 AM UTC on October 16, Bitcoin traded near $82,001.85, up 1.3% over the prior 24 hours, with a daily range of $79,805.99 to $82,508.10.
Bitcoin’s latest price action reflects a classic test of key psychological and technical support.
The cryptocurrency remains roughly 34.9% below its all-time high of $126,080, set on October 6, 2025.
The recent outperformance on the rebound follows a period in which Ethereum underperformed Bitcoin during the initial sell-off.
Corporate and institutional accumulation has also continued in the background.
One example is Bitmine Immersion Technologies, which has steadily added to its Ether holdings, reaching over 4.9% of total supply .
Such treasury strategies illustrate ongoing demand from entities treating Ether as a longer-term reserve asset rather than a pure trading instrument.
The recovery has been orderly rather than explosive.

Daily ranges over recent sessions have frequently spanned several thousand dollars, underscoring elevated short-term volatility even as the broader multi-month range has narrowed relative to earlier 2025 peaks.
Observers note that Bitcoin’s dominance within the total cryptocurrency market has remained relatively stable, consistent with periods when risk appetite is tempered by macro uncertainty.
The primary catalyst for the midweek decline was the release of September 2026 US inflation figures by the Bureau of Labor Statistics .

Bitcoin and Ethereum , the two largest cryptocurrencies by market capitalization, showed modest recoveries in early trading on October 16, 2026, after a sharp midweek sell-off triggered by hotter-than-expected US inflation readings. According to data from CoinGecko as of approximately 05:50 AM UTC on October 16, Bitcoin traded near $82,001.85, up 1.3% over the prior 24 hours, with a daily range of $79,805.99 to $82,508.10. Ethereum stood at $2,444.77, higher by 3.5% in the same period, ranging from $2,324.97 to $2,463.31. The moves followed a session in which both assets tested lower support levels amid renewed questions about the path of US interest rates. Market participants continue to weigh the interplay between macroeconomic data, leveraged positioning in derivatives markets, and longer-term structural demand from institutions and corporate treasuries. While the latest bounce has steadied prices above recent lows, both assets remain well below their respective all-time highs recorded in 2025. Bitcoin’s latest price action reflects a classic test of key psychological and technical support. The asset briefly fell below $80,000 on October 15 before buyers stepped in, as shown in the TradingView chart. At the time of the latest CoinGecko snapshot , Bitcoin’s market capitalization stood at approximately $1.649 trillion, supported by a circulating supply of about 20.099 million coins and 24-hour trading volume near $33.537 billion. The cryptocurrency remains roughly 34.9% below its all-time high of $126,080, set on October 6, 2025. The recovery has been orderly rather than explosive. Daily ranges over recent sessions have frequently spanned several thousand dollars, underscoring elevated short-term volatility even as the broader multi-month range has narrowed relative to earlier 2025 peaks. Observers note that Bitcoin’s dominance within the total cryptocurrency market has remained relatively stable, consistent with periods when risk appetite is tempered by macro uncertainty. Trading activity has concentrated on major centralized exchanges, with volume profiles indicating that the sub-$80,000 dip attracted dip-buying interest from both discretionary traders and some automated strategies. Open interest in perpetual futures has moderated from earlier-week highs, reducing the immediate fuel for further cascading moves in either direction. Ethereum has displayed relatively stronger percentage gains over the latest 24-hour window, climbing 3.5% to $2,444.77 per CoinGecko data. Its market capitalization is approximately $298.59 billion, with 24-hour volume of roughly $14.814 billion and a circulating supply near 122.14 million ETH . The asset trades about 50.6% below its all-time high of $4,946.05 from August 24, 2025. The recent outperformance on the rebound follows a period in which Ethereum underperformed Bitcoin during the initial sell-off. Network activity metrics, including transaction counts and decentralized finance volumes, have remained relatively resilient even as spot prices fluctuated. Corporate and institutional accumulation has also continued in the background. One example is Bitmine Immersion Technologies, which has steadily added to its Ether holdings, reaching over 4.9% of total supply . Such treasury strategies illustrate ongoing demand from entities treating Ether as a longer-term reserve asset rather than a pure trading instrument. Ethereum’s 24-hour range of roughly $2,325 to $2,463 shows it successfully defended support near the lower end of the recent band. Relative strength against Bitcoin has improved modestly over the past day, though the longer-term ETH/BTC ratio remains a focus for traders monitoring capital rotation between the two largest assets. The primary catalyst for the midweek decline was the release of September 2026 US inflation figures by the Bureau of Labor Statistics . The Consumer Price Index (CPI) for All Urban Consumers rose 0.6% on a seasonally adjusted basis in September, bringing the 12-month rate to 3.7%. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the year. These readings exceeded many economists’ expectations and lifted market-implied probabilities of further Federal Reserve tightening before year-end. Higher interest-rate expectations tend to pressure risk assets, including cryptocurrencies, by raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding or lower-yielding instruments and by strengthening the US dollar. The inflation print arrived alongside similar upside surprises in producer prices, reinforcing the narrative that disinflation progress has stalled. In response, Bitcoin and Ethereum both sold off sharply, with the decline amplified by forced liquidations in leveraged derivatives markets. CoinGlass data indicated total crypto liquidations approached or exceeded $900 million to nearly $1 billion over a 24-hour window on October 15, with the large majority occurring in long positions. Ethereum and Bitcoin together accounted for a substantial share of those liquidations, as leveraged traders were stopped out near the session lows. Such liquidation cascades are a recurring feature of crypto markets when prices move quickly against concentrated leveraged positions. Once initial stops are triggered, forced selling can push prices lower, hitting additional stops and creating a feedback loop until new buyers absorb the supply. In this instance, the process appeared to exhaust itself near the $79,800–80,000 area for Bitcoin and corresponding support for Ethereum, after which prices recovered. Funding rates in perpetual futures have remained relatively contained post-event, suggesting that extreme one-sided leverage has been reduced for the moment. Broader market conditions also played a role. Equity markets, particularly in Asia, experienced significant declines around the same period, with some indexes posting large single-day drops. Cryptocurrency prices have shown intermittent correlations with risk assets during periods of macro stress, even as longer-term narratives around digital scarcity and institutional adoption continue to develop. Spot Bitcoin and Ethereum exchange-traded products have seen mixed flows in recent sessions, with some days of net outflows coinciding with the inflation-driven weakness and occasional inflows providing a partial offset. Open interest in perpetual futures has moderated from earlier-week highs, reducing the immediate fuel for further cascading moves in either direction.

So, you put a little mad money into bitcoin a few years ago. Now, your crypto-fueled profit means you have a sweet nest egg to put toward a house.
But can you buy a house with crypto rather than using cash or a traditional mortgage loan? What are the roadblocks? And what about taxes?

President Trump wants the United States to be "the crypto capital of the world." In that spirit, in late June, Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) William J. Pulte ordered Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to "prepare their businesses to count cryptocurrency as an asset for a mortgage."
The FHFA supervises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the government-sponsored companies that fund a major portion of the mortgage industry.

Pulte said the housing system "needs a massive upgrade," adding, "I want people who own cryptocurrency to be able to buy homes like everyone else. I believe cryptocurrency is an asset. I believe Americans should be able to use their crypto if they want to. It's time the housing system caught up."
This signals what could be a fundamental change to how cryptocurrency may be used to qualify for a mortgage.

sources.title: Crypto Price Today: Bitcoin and Ethereum Recover Modestly After Inflation-Driven Dip - The Crypto Times
passages: In response, Bitcoin and Ethereum both sold off sharply, with the decline amplified by forced liquidations in leveraged derivatives markets.
CoinGlass data indicated total crypto liquidations approached or exceeded $900 million to nearly $1 billion over a 24-hour window on October 15, with the large majority occurring in long positions.
Ethereum and Bitcoin together accounted for a substantial share of those liquidations, as leveraged traders were stopped out near the session lows.
Such liquidation cascades are a recurring feature of crypto markets when prices move quickly against concentrated leveraged positions.
Once initial stops are triggered, forced selling can push prices lower, hitting additional stops and creating a feedback loop until new buyers absorb the supply.
In this instance, the process appeared to exhaust itself near the $79,800–80,000 area for Bitcoin and corresponding support for Ethereum, after which prices recovered.
Funding rates in perpetual futures have remained relatively contained post-event, suggesting that extreme one-sided leverage has been reduced for the moment.
The information presented is for informational purposes and does not constitute investment advice.
Ethereum’s 24-hour range of roughly $2,325 to $2,463 shows it successfully defended support near the lower end of the recent band.
Relative strength against Bitcoin has improved modestly over the past day, though the longer-term ETH/BTC ratio remains a focus for traders monitoring capital rotation between the two largest assets.
Looking ahead, market participants will monitor subsequent economic releases, Federal Reserve communications, and any shifts in institutional positioning.
Bitcoin’s ability to hold above the low $80,000s and Ethereum’s capacity to sustain levels above $2,400 will be watched as near-term technical references.

Both assets continue to trade with substantial discounts to their 2025 highs, leaving room for either further consolidation or renewed directional moves depending on incoming data and broader risk sentiment.
According to data from CoinGecko as of approximately 05:50 AM UTC on October 16, Bitcoin traded near $82,001.85, up 1.3% over the prior 24 hours, with a daily range of $79,805.99 to $82,508.10.
Bitcoin’s latest price action reflects a classic test of key psychological and technical support.
The cryptocurrency remains roughly 34.9% below its all-time high of $126,080, set on October 6, 2025.
The recent outperformance on the rebound follows a period in which Ethereum underperformed Bitcoin during the initial sell-off.
Corporate and institutional accumulation has also continued in the background.
One example is Bitmine Immersion Technologies, which has steadily added to its Ether holdings, reaching over 4.9% of total supply .
Such treasury strategies illustrate ongoing demand from entities treating Ether as a longer-term reserve asset rather than a pure trading instrument.
The recovery has been orderly rather than explosive.

Daily ranges over recent sessions have frequently spanned several thousand dollars, underscoring elevated short-term volatility even as the broader multi-month range has narrowed relative to earlier 2025 peaks.
Observers note that Bitcoin’s dominance within the total cryptocurrency market has remained relatively stable, consistent with periods when risk appetite is tempered by macro uncertainty.
The primary catalyst for the midweek decline was the release of September 2026 US inflation figures by the Bureau of Labor Statistics .

Deutsche Bank (NYSE: $DB), Germany's biggest lender, is preparing to launch new crypto custody services. As these dates approach, there are often warnings about billions of dollars' worth of contracts set to expire, with emphasis on a "max pain" price that Bitcoin supposedly gravitates towards.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
So, what happens to the price when these contracts expire?
On Deribit, weekly options expire every Friday at 08:00 UTC, while monthly options expire at the same time on the final Friday of the month.
When contracts expire on Deribit, they settle at an official delivery price, calculated as a 30-minute average of its Bitcoin index.
Options that expire "in the money"—meaning they still hold value at expiration—convert into a corresponding futures contract at the strike price, which then settles in cash.
On October 15, Bitcoin's trading activity showed how quickly market buying and selling can overpower the options calendar.
Bitcoin trades at $82,306, up 30% over two months, but remains down 7% for the year as major options expiries loom.
Market makers who sell options often buy or sell Bitcoin to balance their risk—this practice is known as delta hedging.
Factors such as breaking news, inflows into spot Bitcoin ETFs, or major liquidations can quickly overshadow any options-related impact.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) traders are closely watching two key dates on Deribit, the largest Bitcoin options exchange: a weekly expiry on October 16, 2026, and the major monthly expiry on October 30. As these dates approach, there are often warnings about billions of dollars' worth of contracts set to expire, with emphasis on a "max pain" price that Bitcoin supposedly gravitates towards. As of October 15, Bitcoin is trading at $82,306, having dipped to a 24-hour low of $79,806 before rebounding. This recovery fits a pattern from the past two months, during which Bitcoin has risen by 29.9%. However, it is still down 6.7% for the year and has dropped 26.3% compared to the same time last year. So, what happens to the price when these contracts expire? Does the max pain theory provide any insight? An option is a financial contract that gives the buyer the right to buy or sell Bitcoin at a predetermined price, known as the strike price, before a specific expiration date. A call option lets the buyer purchase Bitcoin at the strike price, gaining value when Bitcoin's price rises above it. Conversely, a put option lets you sell at the strike price, gaining value when Bitcoin's price dips below it. Every option has an expiry date, which is when the contract either settles with value or becomes worthless. On Deribit, weekly options expire every Friday at 08:00 UTC, while monthly options expire at the same time on the final Friday of the month. In October, this means contracts expire at 4 a.m. Eastern Time, just hours before U.S. stock markets open. When contracts expire on Deribit, they settle at an official delivery price, calculated as a 30-minute average of its Bitcoin index. This method makes it harder for a single large trade to sway the settlement price. Options that expire "in the money"—meaning they still hold value at expiration—convert into a corresponding futures contract at the strike price, which then settles in cash. Expiry timing also affects market liquidity, as Bitcoin trading volume tends to drop over the weekend. When hedges are unwound at settlement, the market enters the weekend with fewer significant orders on both sides. Max pain refers to the strike price where the total value of all outstanding options contracts is lowest for option buyers. Essentially, it is the price where the sellers, usually market makers, face the smallest overall loss. Traders identify this price by calculating the total value of all open calls and puts at every potential settlement price and selecting the strike price with the lowest total. The expected price pull around max pain stems from hedging activities. Market makers who sell options often buy or sell Bitcoin to balance their risk—this practice is known as delta hedging. As expiry approaches, this hedging typically centers on strikes with high open interest, which can help keep price within a narrow range. After settlement, market makers often unwind these hedges, which can lead to larger price moves in the days following a large expiry. However, max pain is a tendency, not a certainty, and many expiries settle far from this predicted price. Factors such as breaking news, inflows into spot Bitcoin ETFs, or major liquidations can quickly overshadow any options-related impact. The October 16 contract reflects a weekly expiry characterized by shorter-term positions and typically carries less open interest than a monthly expiry. In contrast, the October 30 monthly expiry reflects a larger buildup of positions that traders accumulate over weeks, making it the month's largest expiry. Traders evaluate each expiry using various indicators. Notional value is the total dollar value of the Bitcoin the contracts cover, while open interest tallies the number of contracts still outstanding. Meanwhile, the put/call ratio compares open puts to open calls, with a ratio above 1 indicating more traders are seeking downside protection than upside potential. Max pain, lastly, is the strike price where option buyers would collectively realize the smallest gains. CoinGlass and Deribit update these metrics for every expiry, and the figures can change daily as traders adjust their positions. Therefore, the October 30 expiry data might shift significantly through October 29. The most valuable comparison occurs in the final days when traders can see how far Bitcoin's current price is from the max pain strike. On October 15, Bitcoin's trading activity showed how quickly market buying and selling can overpower the options calendar. The price fluctuated between $79,806 and $82,306 in a single day. The October 16 weekly expiry is expected to have minimal impact, while the October 30 monthly expiry could keep Bitcoin price near max pain as the settlement date approaches. Even then, any pull will likely be modest, with larger price movements typically occurring after the settlement. Additionally, stable stock market conditions could amplify options' impact, as the VIX—the measure of expected S&P 500 volatility—was at a normal level of 16.9 on October 14. The $79,806 low from October 15 is the level to watch. Holding above it through the October 30 settlement would show buyers kept control, while a close below it could mean unwinding hedges removed support, giving the rally since mid-August its first serious test. Expiry timing also affects market liquidity, as Bitcoin trading volume tends to drop over the weekend. When hedges are unwound at settlement, the market enters the weekend with fewer significant orders on both sides.

Max pain refers to the strike price where the total value of all outstanding options contracts is lowest for option buyers. Essentially, it is the price where the sellers, usually market makers, face the smallest overall loss. Traders identify this price by calculating the total value of all open calls and puts at every potential settlement price and selecting the strike price with the lowest total.

The expected price pull around max pain stems from hedging activities. Market makers who sell options often buy or sell Bitcoin to balance their risk—this practice is known as delta hedging. As expiry approaches, this hedging typically centers on strikes with high open interest, which can help keep price within a narrow range.

After settlement, market makers often unwind these hedges, which can lead to larger price moves in the days following a large expiry. However, max pain is a tendency, not a certainty, and many expiries settle far from this predicted price. Factors such as breaking news, inflows into spot Bitcoin ETFs , or major liquidations can quickly overshadow any options-related impact .

The October 16 contract reflects a weekly expiry characterized by shorter-term positions and typically carries less open interest than a monthly expiry. In contrast, the October 30 monthly expiry reflects a larger buildup of positions that traders accumulate over weeks, making it the month’s largest expiry.

Traders evaluate each expiry using various indicators. Notional value is the total dollar value of the Bitcoin the contracts cover, while open interest tallies the number of contracts still outstanding.

Meanwhile, the put/call ratio compares open puts to open calls, with a ratio above 1 indicating more traders are seeking downside protection than upside potential. Max pain, lastly, is the strike price where option buyers would collectively realize the smallest gains.

CoinGlass and Deribit update these metrics for every expiry, and the figures can change daily as traders adjust their positions. Therefore, the October 30 expiry data might shift significantly through October 29. The most valuable comparison occurs in the final days when traders can see how far Bitcoin’s current price is from the max pain strike.
On October 15, Bitcoin’s trading activity showed how quickly market buying and selling can overpower the options calendar. The price fluctuated between $79,806 and $82,306 in a single day.

The October 16 weekly expiry is expected to have minimal impact, while the October 30 monthly expiry could keep Bitcoin price near max pain as the settlement date approaches. Even then, any pull will likely be modest, with larger price movements typically occurring after the settlement. Additionally, stable stock market conditions could amplify options’ impact, as the VIX—the measure of expected S&P 500 volatility—was at a normal level of 16.9 on October 14.

The $79,806 low from October 15 is the level to watch. Holding above it through the October 30 settlement would show buyers kept control, while a close below it could mean unwinding hedges removed support, giving the rally since mid-August its first serious test .

passages: Sprouts Farmers Market's first-ever chief technology officer, Jim Bahrenburg, has resigned, according to a Monday filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Bahrenburg's departure marks the first confirmed C-suite change since the grocery company announced in early September that CEO Jack Sinclair plans to step down from the top role.
The grocer named Nick Konat, Sprouts' president and chief operating officer, as its next CEO, effective Jan.
Sinclair will become the chain's executive chairman at that time.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Bahrenburg joined Sprouts in September 2023 , stepping into a newly created C-suite role at the company.

His retail career also included serving as Good Food Holdings' CIO from November 2019 to August 2023 and more than a dozen years with 99 Cent Only Stores, according to his bio page on Sprouts' website.

Bahrenburg, who spent three years overseeing the strategic direction and management of Sprouts' technology, will continue to serve as an advisor to the specialty grocer through March 31, 2027, to support an orderly transition, the filing noted.
Sprouts did not respond to a request for comment by press time about who will succeed Bahrenburg.

sources.title: Better Buy After the Rebound: Chainlink or Bitcoin? One Is Up 13% This Month. - Yahoo Finance
passages: Chainlink (CRYPTO: LINK) has outperformed Bitcoin in the recent market rebound, rising 13% in the 30 days leading up to October 15, 2026, versus Bitcoin's 8% gain (CRYPTO: BTC).
This has left potential investors wondering which coin is the better buy—Chainlink or Bitcoin.
At its current price of $12.54, Chainlink needs a remarkable 320% increase to rebound back to its all-time high of $52.70.
Conversely, Bitcoin, trading at about $82,159, requires a 53% gain to reach its record high of $126,080.
On August 31, 2026, CME Group ( NASDAQ: CME ) and CF Benchmarks introduced the CME Emerging Crypto Index—a ten-coin benchmark that excludes Bitcoin and Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH).
While the index includes Chainlink, its weight distribution is skewed.

Coins like BNB (CRYPTO: BNB), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), and Hyperliquid (CRYPTO: HYPE) account for about 93% of the index, leaving the remaining six coins, including Chainlink, with just 7.3% of the total weight.
However, this buying momentum stalled, with no new inflows recorded on October 13 and 14.
As of October 14, these Chainlink funds held about $220.5 million in total net assets.
In comparison, spot Bitcoin ETFs boasted a much higher figure of about $104.8 billion.
So, after this rebound, which cryptocurrency offers new buyers a better chance of a full recovery?
A decline below the October low of $80,315 could jeopardize much of its recent recovery.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

Bitcoin ETFs experienced substantial inflows, with nearly $999 million coming in on September 21, and remained positive in every session from September 17 to September 29, with Bitcoin ending September at $83,556, up from August's close of $78,563.
However, October has seen more erratic Bitcoin flows.
On the other hand, Bitcoin has already risen 43% from June 2026's closing figure of $58,524 to its September close, showing how quickly it can regain value once institutional investment returns.
Currently, no futures are listed for this index, meaning funds have no investment vehicle to track it.
The index's first rebalance is set for December 2026, and a potential futures launch could be a major catalyst for investment in Chainlink.
However, it would need to more than quadruple from its current value and still trade below the $18.06 it reached on October 15, 2025.
Chainlink could turn attractive if ETFs regain steady inflows and LINK closes above $18.06 before CME's December index rebalance.
Chainlink operates as an oracle network, providing essential external data, such as asset prices, to blockchains that can't access data outside their own system.
This capability is vital for applications like lending platforms, which rely on accurate price feeds to evaluate their collateral, and they pay for this data using LINK tokens.

coreStoryFacts.text: Chainlink (CRYPTO: LINK) has outperformed Bitcoin in the recent market rebound, rising 13% in the 30 days leading up to October 15, 2026, versus Bitcoin's 8% gain (CRYPTO: BTC).
This has left potential investors wondering which coin is the better buy—Chainlink or Bitcoin.
At its current price of $12.54, Chainlink needs a remarkable 320% increase to rebound back to its all-time high of $52.70.
Conversely, Bitcoin, trading at about $82,159, requires a 53% gain to reach its record high of $126,080.
On August 31, 2026, CME Group ( NASDAQ: CME ) and CF Benchmarks introduced the CME Emerging Crypto Index—a ten-coin benchmark that excludes Bitcoin and Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH).
While the index includes Chainlink, its weight distribution is skewed.

Coins like BNB (CRYPTO: BNB), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), and Hyperliquid (CRYPTO: HYPE) account for about 93% of the index, leaving the remaining six coins, including Chainlink, with just 7.3% of the total weight.
However, this buying momentum stalled, with no new inflows recorded on October 13 and 14.
As of October 14, these Chainlink funds held about $220.5 million in total net assets.
In comparison, spot Bitcoin ETFs boasted a much higher figure of about $104.8 billion.
So, after this rebound, which cryptocurrency offers new buyers a better chance of a full recovery?
A decline below the October low of $80,315 could jeopardize much of its recent recovery.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

Bitcoin ETFs experienced substantial inflows, with nearly $999 million coming in on September 21, and remained positive in every session from September 17 to September 29, with Bitcoin ending September at $83,556, up from August's close of $78,563.
However, October has seen more erratic Bitcoin flows.
On the other hand, Bitcoin has already risen 43% from June 2026's closing figure of $58,524 to its September close, showing how quickly it can regain value once institutional investment returns.
Currently, no futures are listed for this index, meaning funds have no investment vehicle to track it.
The index's first rebalance is set for December 2026, and a potential futures launch could be a major catalyst for investment in Chainlink.
However, it would need to more than quadruple from its current value and still trade below the $18.06 it reached on October 15, 2025.
Chainlink could turn attractive if ETFs regain steady inflows and LINK closes above $18.06 before CME's December index rebalance.
Chainlink operates as an oracle network, providing essential external data, such as asset prices, to blockchains that can't access data outside their own system.

sources.title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again - Ars Technica
passages: Nine years after first trying to resurrect the Roadster , Tesla is apparently trying again.

CEO Elon Musk might have relocated its HQ to Texas, but yet again he has returned to California’s showbiz industry to hawk his wares; last time it was a Hollywood back lot for the remote-controlled Cybercab demo , last night it was decades-old stunt technology to make a show car do tricks in the air.
And right now, that’s the McMurtry Spéirling, which looks like a miniaturized Batmobile (the good Michael Keaton one) and which is capable of generating up to 3.5 lateral Gs.
The best Tesla claims for the new Roadster is 2 Gs.
Oh, and the Spéirling will most definitely drive upside down.
Musk claims that the Roadster will go into production by 2028.

But the CEO has a long and glorious history of overpromising and underdelivering; in 2017 he told attendees at the previous launch that “We are making it now.” Using the company’s referral program, some people were in line to receive two free cars.
But those free cars never showed up, and neither did the ones that people put down $50,000 deposits for; last year Sam Altman discovered how hard it can be to get that money back .
But as Musk has told us time and again, Tesla is no longer a car company .
Currently, he seems more interested in merging Tesla with SpaceX , claiming synergies having to do with AI despite most of his AI-derived revenues coming from renting GPU time to others.
But a merger would give SpaceX a backdoor into the S&P 500 index, which rejected the rocket company in June, as it requires several consecutive profitable quarters for inclusion.
Apparently, that could happen before the end of the year.
At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation.
Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years.
With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information.
After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

The battery pack uses the troubled 4680 cells it has been trying to scale up in-house; customer complaints of poor performance were presumably the driving force behind developing what the company says is a special battery chemistry just for this model.
Some of the performance claims are even more grandiose than nine years ago.
Now, Musk claims a planned top speed of 383 mph (616 km/h), with a 0-60 mph time of 0.8 seconds.
And as with the last time this happened , there are already other EVs on sale that are more capable than Tesla’s vaporware claims.

Its stratospheric valuation was predicated in large part upon promises of constant growth, something that perhaps seemed possible when its market share was near total and there was little competition for EVs.
But now Europe and China have hundreds of models to choose from—only two of which are offered by Tesla.
The Models 3 and Y are both increasingly aged, and Tesla has shown little ability to innovate rapidly like the Chinese brands that have taken so much of its sales away there.
In fact, it might even leave the Chinese market .
Meanwhile, Tesla’s core business remains in trouble.
Even in quarters with decent sales, its profits are vanishing as costs rise and selling prices drop .
And most recently, sales have not been decent .

Unusually, Tesla says it stuck with rear-wheel drive for the new electric vehicle. The battery pack uses the troubled 4680 cells it has been trying to scale up in-house; customer complaints of poor performance were presumably the driving force behind developing what the company says is a special battery chemistry just for this model.

Some of the performance claims are even more grandiose than nine years ago. Now, Musk claims a planned top speed of 383 mph (616 km/h), with a 0-60 mph time of 0.8 seconds. And as with the last time this happened , there are already other EVs on sale that are more capable than Tesla’s vaporware claims.

And right now, that’s the McMurtry Spéirling, which looks like a miniaturized Batmobile (the good Michael Keaton one) and which is capable of generating up to 3.5 lateral Gs. The best Tesla claims for the new Roadster is 2 Gs. Oh, and the Spéirling will most definitely drive upside down.

The Spéirling has also set a faster lap time around the Top Gear test track than an F1 car, blitzed the Goodwood Hill Climb record, and I’m pretty sure would demolish Volkswagen’s untouchable Pikes Peak time if it gave it a shot. McMurtry has sold at least 24 of the planned 100-car production run.

Musk claims that the Roadster will go into production by 2028. But the CEO has a long and glorious history of overpromising and underdelivering; in 2017 he told attendees at the previous launch that “We are making it now.” Using the company’s referral program, some people were in line to receive two free cars. But those free cars never showed up, and neither did the ones that people put down $50,000 deposits for; last year Sam Altman discovered how hard it can be to get that money back .
And it’s not like there’s actually much of a market for very expensive, very fast EVs: hypercar buyers want noise and an emotional connection, and they don’t get that from an EV .

Meanwhile, Tesla’s core business remains in trouble. Even in quarters with decent sales, its profits are vanishing as costs rise and selling prices drop . And most recently, sales have not been decent .

Its stratospheric valuation was predicated in large part upon promises of constant growth, something that perhaps seemed possible when its market share was near total and there was little competition for EVs. But now Europe and China have hundreds of models to choose from—only two of which are offered by Tesla. The Models 3 and Y are both increasingly aged, and Tesla has shown little ability to innovate rapidly like the Chinese brands that have taken so much of its sales away there. In fact, it might even leave the Chinese market .

But as Musk has told us time and again, Tesla is no longer a car company . Currently, he seems more interested in merging Tesla with SpaceX , claiming synergies having to do with AI despite most of his AI-derived revenues coming from renting GPU time to others. But a merger would give SpaceX a backdoor into the S&P 500 index, which rejected the rocket company in June, as it requires several consecutive profitable quarters for inclusion. Should Musk succeed, he will have access to billions of dollars from passive investment funds that invest retirement accounts in the S&P 500. Apparently, that could happen before the end of the year.
